question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the reason rent is already being paid on the new passport office in Cork; and whether the new office will include a passport printer.
reply:
The Office of Public Works (OPW), in conjunction with my Department, is progressing the development of new office accommodation for the Passport Service in Cork. Any query relating to the rental of this accommodation is a matter for the OPW, as the leaseholder for the property.
The Passport Online service offers citizens the ability to apply online for their passport 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Approximately 97% of all passport applications are now made through Passport Online.
The public offices of the Passport Service in Cork and Dublin 2 operate an Urgent Appointment service for renewal applications. During 2026, there were an average of 240 urgent appointments for a four-day turnaround service available in Cork each week. In 2025, just 15.6% of appointments available in Cork were booked.
The Passport Service operates three passport book printing machines: two machines located in the main production facility at the Balbriggan campus and one at the Dublin 2 Passport Office. The printing and dispatch of passports is a highly automated process in what is, essentially, an industrial production system.
The Passport Service estimates the initial capital cost of purchasing and installing new printer and mailing machine to be approximately €5.3 million. In addition to the capital investment, these highly sophisticated machines require expert engineers to be on-site while the machines are in operation to maintain and service the machines and repair them when necessary. reply:

Maintaining strong, stable and predictable economic relationships matters enormously for an open economy like ours.

question: Deputy James O'Connor asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade her response to recent Russian hybrid attacks against the European Union and its Member States.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 47 and 90 together.
The Government has strongly condemned Russia’s attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport in August.
This activity is part of a clear trend. It forms part of a broader, coordinated, and long-standing hybrid campaign aimed at threatening and undermining the security, resilience and democratic foundations of the EU, its Member States and its partners.
In response to the Leipzig incident, I expressed my full solidarity with Germany, and with all Member States affected by Russia’s reckless and increasingly frequent hybrid attacks. I discussed the issue with the HRVP, Kaja Kallas, and my German and other EU counterparts at the meeting of EU Foreign Ministers I hosted in Druid's Glen in early September.
The Ambassador of the Russian Federation was summoned by senior officials of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade on 3 September to hear expression of Ireland’s strong condemnation. Many of our EU partners also did so. Russia’s attempts to divide us and to weaken our support for Ukraine will not succeed.
Ireland is extremely concerned at the continued increased in hybrid activity. Russia’s actions threaten the security of EU citizens, as well as regional stability and international peace.
We support the full use of all tools available to prevent, deter, and respond to Russia’s hybrid activities, including through sanctions.

question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade to provide an update on the plans for a new passport office in Cork; the anticipated timeline for its opening; the additional capacity and public services that are planned; and whether urgent passport appointments will be available.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 84 and 89 together.
The Passport Service received 44,464 passport applications from County Cork between January and August 2026, comprising 9,067 first-time applications and 35,397 renewal applications.
This compares with 46,240 passport applications during the corresponding period in 2025, of which 10,300 were first-time applications and 35,940 were renewals.
In 2026 passport applications from County Cork in 2026 decreased by 1,776 applications, or 3.8%, compared with the same period in 2025. First-time applications decreased by 1,233, or 12%, while renewals decreased by 543, or 1.5%.
The Office of Public Works (OPW), in conjunction with my Department, is progressing the development of new office accommodation for the Passport Service in Cork. Any query relating to the timeline for the opening of this accommodation is a matter for the OPW.
This new passport office, which will be located at Navigation Square in Cork City, will include a public office well-equipped to serve the needs of citizens in the region.
The Cork Passport Office will continue to provide an Urgent Appointment Service on the same basis as is currently offered in Cork. Customers who need to have their passport renewed urgently can book a four day appointment at the public counter in Cork. There are currently 240 Urgent Appointment slots available each week at the Cork Passport Office.

question: Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade for a report on her attendance at the recent British-Irish Association annual conference.
reply:
I attended the annual British Irish Association conference in Oxford on 4 September which was held under Chatham House rules.
I was pleased to deliver opening remarks and to participate in an interactive question and answer session with participants. In my remarks, I spoke about how relations across these islands are being reshaped by the changes we are seeing in the international environment and the shared challenges these changes present us all.
I recalled the ambitious agenda for bilateral relations between the Irish and UK government, in the shape of the UK-Ireland Joint Statement.
I also spoke about our work to unlock the full potential of the Good Friday Agreement through the work of the North South bodies and through the Shared Island Initiative. I discussed the implementation of the Joint Framework on Legacy, which we agreed with the UK Government last year.
I am pleased that this year the BIA was once more designated as a Strategic Partner of the Reconciliation Fund which will provide funding of €50,000 per year for the next three years.
The BIA conference remains as an important event in the calendar of British-Irish relations which promotes mutual understanding and good relations between the people of our islands, and with a valuable focus on Northern Ireland.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the actions she and her Department have taken diplomatically at EU and UN level to pursue global action on climate commitments and the Paris Agreement following the heatwaves, flooding, and other extreme weather events globally in recent months.
reply:
This year has seen devastating heatwaves, floods, droughts and storms affecting communities across every region of the world. The summer wildfires in Europe and the recent devastation in Nepal are stark reminders that climate change is not a future threat but a present reality, underscoring the urgency of global action.
At EU and UN level, Ireland continues to advocate for ambitious implementation of the Paris Agreement and stronger international action to address the effects of climate change. As EU Presidency, Ireland is leading engagement with EU Member States, the European Commission and international partners in advance of COP31 in Antalya in November. We are working to build consensus around outcomes on emissions reduction, adaptation, climate finance and loss and damage, with the objective of keeping the Paris Agreement's 1.5°C goal within reach.
At the United Nations, including during UN General Assembly High-Level Week, we have engaged with UN partners, fellow Member States and vulnerable countries on preparations for COP31. Ireland consistently advocates for the prioritisation of adaptation finance for Least Developed Countries and Small Island Developing States, with a particular emphasis on grant-based support.
This is reflected across Ireland's own international climate finance with, 89% of which supports adaptation, helping vulnerable communities to strengthen their resilience and prepare for a changing climate.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the steps her Department is taking to reach the 0.7% goal for overseas development aid; and the engagements she has had with other EU member states on increasing their aid budgets.
reply:
The Government remains committed to the United Nations target to provide 0.7% of Gross National Income (GNI) in Official Development Assistance (ODA). This commitment was reaffirmed in A Better World, Ireland's international development policy and in the Programme for Government which commits to increases in ODA, towards the 0.7% target.
Ireland’s total Official Development Assistance (ODA) amounted to €1.88 billion in 2025, representing 0.44% of Gross National Income (GNI). In recent years, the Government has consistently increased the allocation for the Irish Aid programme managed by the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, which works to address the needs of some of the world’s poorest or most climate-exposed countries and communities and those living in areas affected by conflict.
The Budget 2026 allocation for the programme was just over €840 million, the highest ever in the 52-year history of Ireland's development programme. Ahead of Budget 2027, I am working with colleagues to ensure an ODA allocation which can continue to deliver on Ireland’s commitment to playing our role in the fight to end global poverty and hunger and to reaching the furthest behind first.
We have ensured a strong focus on development cooperation and humanitarian assistance during our EU Presidency, both in internal EU discussions and at the United Nations.

question: Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the way in which Ireland’s Presidency of the Council of the European Union is being used to showcase Galway and other regions outside Dublin; and the opportunities being provided for regional communities to participate in and benefit from Ireland’s Presidency.
reply:
Ireland assumed the Presidency of the Council of the European Union on 1 July this year. The Presidency is an opportunity for Ireland to play an important role in leading and shaping the EU’s policy and legislative agenda, and the Government has made a firm commitment to deliver a successful Presidency.
In the Programme for Government, we committed to bringing some of the high-level meetings of our Presidency to cities and counties across Ireland, ensuring that the entire country benefits from the profile the Presidency brings.
Overall, we expect to host more than 270 Presidency events in Ireland, with approximately a quarter of these taking place regionally. To date, 95 meetings and events have been held in locations including Galway, Clare, Cork, Dublin, Donegal, Kildare, Kilkenny, Mayo, Meath, Monaghan, Westmeath, Wexford and Wicklow.
It is anticipated that five official Presidency events and meetings will take place in Galway over the course of the Presidency, facilitating discussions across a diverse range of policy areas, including environment, education and transport.
There are also ten Associated Presidency Events currently planned for Galway, organised by civil society, academia, business and representative bodies. Aligned with the themes and priorities of Ireland’s EU Presidency, these events promote and enable wider local participation in the Presidency.

question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade to report on her Department's engagements, if any, with the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in relation to the Ireland-Palestine scholarship programme which the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade co-administers; if she believes the programme has been undermined by the refusal of visas to Palestinian students offered places under the programme.
reply:
Since the start of the Gaza crisis, my Department has facilitated nearly 400 people to exit Gaza and travel to Ireland, including students taking up studies in Ireland’s Higher Education Institutions, some of whom won places on the Ireland-Palestine Scholarship Programme.
All arrivals have been facilitated through ongoing and close coordination between my Department, the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, the Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science, and Irish Higher Education Institutions.
Since the initiation of the Ireland Palestine Scholarship Programme in 2019, 176 students from Palestine have benefited. For the academic year 2026/2027, my Department offered 30 places on the Programme, of which students were able to take up 24.
I understand that one student from Gaza was unsuccessful in their visa application.
While I cannot comment on the details of individual applications, the Deputy will appreciate that any individual seeking assistance to leave Gaza must first be in possession of a valid visa to travel to Ireland. Visa policy is a matter for the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, which assesses each visa application on its own merits.

question: Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if she will provide an update on the British Government's response to the State's ongoing request for full disclosure and access to all relevant documents concerning the Dublin and Monaghan bombings of 17 May 1974.
reply:
This year marks the 52nd anniversary of the Dublin Monaghan bombings. My thoughts are first and foremost with the families who continue to seek the truth of what happened to their loved ones on that day and it was important to me that my Department was represented at the commemoration on Talbot Street in May.
In relation to contact with the British Government, I have spoken with the new Secretary of State for Northern Ireland, Christ Bryant MP, a number of times since his appointment in July.
We have discussed our key priorities for Northern Ireland in the months ahead, particularly the need to progress the implementation of the Joint Framework on the Legacy of the Troubles, agreed last year by the two Governments. Reciprocal co-operation is at the heart of the Joint Framework, which commits the British Government to provide "cooperation to Ireland for investigations, inquiries and inquests" in this jurisdiction.
The Government has long-standing requests in place to allow access by an independent, international judicial figure to all original documents held by the British Government relating to the Dublin and Monaghan bombings. These requests arise from successive all-party motions adopted by this House.

question: Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the way in which she has raised the issue to advance the case for Irish reunification internationally.
reply:
The position of the Government on Irish re-unification is determined by Article 3 of the Constitution, as amended by the people in 1998 to incorporate the framework set out in the Good Friday Agreement.
The Programme for Government states clearly that this Government is committed to the unity of the Irish people. This can only be achieved through a sustained focus on and investment in reconciliation. We remain steadfast in implementing the Good Friday Agreement in full and supporting the functioning of all of its institutions.
In my discussions with international partners, I am heartened that there is a continued interest in the peace process and on furthering reconciliation in Northern Ireland today.
Securing the peace through the Good Friday Agreement would not have been possible without the support of those international partners.
Our commitment to unlocking the full potential of the Agreement, includes addressing the legacy of the Troubles and through the Shared Island Initiative, to which we have allocated €2 billion through to 2035. Our whole-of-government approach is building a more connected, prosperous and reconciled island for people North and South. In the event of a future referendum, we will make all necessary preparations within the terms of the Constitution and the principles and procedures of the Agreement.

question: Deputy Cathy Bennett asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if she will consider opening a passport office in the North.
reply:
The Passport Online service offers citizens the ability to apply online for their passport 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Over 97% of all passport applications are now made through Passport Online which is available to 100% of all applicants globally. It is worth noting that just 1% of passports issue through the public counter in Dublin.
Demand for passports from citizens resident in Northern Ireland remains steady. To date in 2026, over 97% of applications from citizens resident in Northern Ireland have been made through Passport Online, compared with 91% in 2025.
Last December, the Passport Service launched a new Passport Assist Service to support citizens who do not wish to use Passport Online channel and assist them to make a paper passport application. Citizens can call the dedicated Passport Assist number to receive a personalised paper form, along with a bespoke list of documents required, which they can post back to the Passport Service through their local post office. This all-island service has enhanced the paper application route by offering direct assistance to citizens.
In terms of any proposed additional passport office, there are considerable financial implications to consider. question: Deputy Donnchadh Ó Laoghaire asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the position regarding the war in Iran and the Gulf region.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 21 and 76 together.
I am very concerned by the resumption of hostilities between Iran and the United States, following the expiry of the negotiating period provided for under the 17 June Memorandum of Understanding. Ireland has consistently maintained that the best way forward is a return by both sides to meaningful, good-faith negotiations aimed at restoring regional peace and stability.
I have remained in contact with my counterparts on the confict in the Gulf, including during High Level Week at the United Nations General Assembly in New York last week. The situation in the region was also discussed at the EU informal Foreign Affairs Council meeting in Wicklow in September. Attacks by Iran risk further undermining regional stability. Ireland calls on all parties to exercise restraint and uphold international law, including the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure. Any loss of civilian life through conflict is unacceptable and must be avoided. We extend our sympathy to the families of those who have lost loved ones.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if her Department has been in contact with Irish citizens in Turkey, following the recent crackdowns.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 29, 46 and 75 together.
I am deeply concerned about recent measures, including legal proceedings and arrests, against LGBTIQ+ organisations and persons in Türkiye. As an EU candidate country, member of the Council of Europe, and a party to international human rights instruments, Türkiye is expected to uphold the highest democratic standards and to ensure the respect of fundamental rights for all, including for LGBTIQ+ persons.
Every person, regardless of sexual orientation, gender identity, or any other characteristic, is entitled to equality, dignity and the full enjoyment of their human rights. The promotion and protection of the rights of LGBTIQ+ persons is a domestic and foreign policy priority for Ireland, and this is reflected in our campaign for membership of the UN Human Rights Council, where defending the rights of LGBTIQ+ persons is one of our five thematic priorities.
Ireland continues to support initiatives in the EU and other international fora which promote and protect the rights of LGBTIQ+ people, and which condemn violence and discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Ireland stands in full solidarity with LGBTIQ+ persons and their allies in Türkiye. As part of ongoing bilateral engagement, Ireland raises human rights issues, including regarding LGBTIQ+ persons, with the Turkish authorities.

reply:
I am pleased to inform the Deputy that I launched Ireland’s third Diaspora Strategy covering the period 2026-2030 at the Global Irish Civic Forum on the 30th of April. In developing our new strategy, I led the largest ever consultation with the Irish abroad, including over 27 in-person meetings, and the first ever online consultation, the Global Irish Survey, which ran throughout the summer of 2025.
The outcome of this extensive consultation process is a strategy that sets out 23 commitments built around the challenges and opportunities that were shared with us.
Supporting the most vulnerable remains at the heart of this new strategy, as is our commitment to partner with Irish communities overseas to promote our culture, music, identity and sport, and to showcase the values of a modern and diverse Ireland to a global audience.
We also address the particular challenges facing those who are considering emigrating, those who are newly arrived abroad and those looking to return.
The strategy recognises the real appetite among the diaspora for supporting our trade and economic priorities. We will step up our engagements to embrace these influential networks and vital insights in support of accessing new markets, securing Foreign Direct Investment and driving job creation and innovation.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the way in which she is promoting diplomatic and trade relations with Barbados.
reply:
Ireland is committed to promoting its diplomatic and trade relations with Barbados, including in the context of our EU Presidency.
Under our Second Strategy for Latin America and the Caribbean we opened Ireland’s Office for the Caribbean, based in Miami in 2024. The Office works to strengthen diplomatic, trade, and cultural links with the Caribbean and Barbados. Barbados established an Embassy in Dublin in 2024, which was officially opened during the visit of Prime Minister Mia Mottley in May this year. Barbados was also a central part of our Ireland-Latin America and Caribbean Trade Horizons Forum, a high-level trade promotion event co-hosted by my Department and the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment in May. The Foreign Minister of Barbados was the keynote speaker and a delegation from Invest Barbados also participated. During the event, a Memorandum of Understanding on an Air Services Agreement with Barbados was exchanged. Ireland continues to promote trade with Barbados, and will support the ‘Invest Barbados’ Ireland Investment event in Barbados in November this year. question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if her Department has assessed whether Ireland is out of step with other European Union member states in not maintaining a trade or representative office in Taiwan; and if consideration has been given to reopening an Irish Trade and Cultural Office in Taipei to strengthen economic, trade, cultural and links with Taiwan.
reply:
Ireland, along with our EU partners, adheres to the One China Policy. This means that we recognise the People's Republic of China as the sole legal government of China, and that we do not have diplomatic relations with Taiwan. However, the absence of diplomatic of relations does not preclude the development of economic, cultural and people-to-people connections.
My Department has never maintained an office in Taipei. IDA Ireland, the agency responsible for attracting foreign direct investment to Ireland, previously had an office in Taipei but it was closed in 2011 solely based on business reasons. IDA Ireland now manages the Taiwanese market from its Singapore office, and Enterprise Ireland, the agency responsible for enterprise development, manages the market from its office in Hong Kong.
I am aware that some EU Member States have trade offices in Taipei, and I note that the EU has maintained its European Economic and Trade Office in Taipei since 2003. However, it is important to note that decisions on the opening of new offices by the Government are taken on the basis of need and how best to promote our own interests abroad rather than to match the approach of other countries.
There are currently no plans to establish a trade and cultural office in Taipei. The establishment of new offices is always kept under review. The opening of new offices is a resource-intensive process. Decisions are evaluated on the basis of a number of factors, including cost-benefit considerations

question: Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade to provide an update on her recent engagements regarding the EU-Israel Association Agreement; and the possible sanctions to be taken against Israel on the basis of its actions against the Palestinian people.
reply:
The Israel-Palestine conflict, and the defence of the two-State solution, is a key priority during our Presidency. We are working to ensure that focus is maintained on the dire humanitarian needs in Gaza and the appalling situation in the West Bank.
In particular, we are continuing to press for appropriate action in response to egregious Israeli breaches of international law, human rights and democratic principles. The situation in Gaza and the West Bank was discussed at the Informal Meeting of EU Foreign Ministers that I hosted in Wicklow on 1-2 September.
Ireland’s long-standing position is that the EU-Israel Association Agreement should be suspended, or at a minimum that the trade elements should be suspended. A number of other Member States have supported Ireland’s call for stronger collective EU action, and this is a call that Ireland will continue to make.
In addition, while we have moved ahead at the national level with our own Israeli Settlements Act, Ireland continues to lead the call for an EU-wide prohibition on trade with Israeli settlements. The Government remains clear that collective action at the EU level is the strongest and most effective route to prohibit trade with Israeli settlements.
I have repeatedly called for the European Commission to bring forward proposals in this regard, on the basis of the EU's Common Commercial Policy, to ensure the EU is in compliance with its international obligations.

question: Deputy Donnchadh Ó Laoghaire asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade her views on the current situation in Lebanon and the Government's position regarding same.
reply:
Ireland has welcomed the trilateral framework agreement reached between the US, Israel and Lebanon, and the Israeli commitment to begin withdrawing from Lebanon. Its implementation by all concerned is essential if a sustainable peace is to be achieved.
However it is clear that the ongoing attacks by Israel in southern Lebanon are not helping and are undermining the prospect of a meaningful peace. This continued violation of Lebanese sovereignty is unacceptable.
Ireland has been clear that Israel needs to fully withdraw its military presence from southern Lebanon. The creation of a 'buffer zone' akin to that used by the IDF in Gaza is completely unacceptable, undermines the fragile ceasefire agreement and jeopardises the process of rebuilding Lebanon.
Ireland has consistently and unequivocally condemned Hezbollah for its attacks on Israel, and has stressed the need for it to take steps towards disarmament immediately.
All sides have an obligation to maintain the ceasefire and abide by UN Security Council Resolution 1701.
Ireland remains committed to supporting the security forces in fulfilling their role in securing Lebanon and encourages all political parties’ participation in discussions to ensure a full functioning democracy.
Ireland will continue to work with Lebanon, and with EU and international partners to support Lebanon’s future peace and security. I made this point when I met with the Lebanese Foreign Minister in New York, during UN High Level Week.

question: Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade her response to the recent removal of EU sanctions from a number of Russian businesspeople.

question: Deputy Cormac Devlin asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade for a report on the Shared Island Civic Society Fund.
reply:
Since its launch in 2023, the Shared Island Civic Society Fund (SICSF) has provided some €5 million supporting 171 projects across the island of Ireland to encourage practical North-South cooperation and engagement. The maximum grant awarded to any project is €50,00.
The Fund is an important component of the Shared Island initiative, which supports collaboration on joint projects between grassroots community organisations and their cross-border counterparts with the overall objective of strengthening North-South civic, economic and political links.
Some of the sectors supported by the SICSF to date include: Business and Social Enterprise, Community and Voluntary Sector, Environmental Awareness, Migrant Communities, Sport, Trade Unions, Women’s Groups and Youth Engagement.
The SICSF is now in its second, three-year cycle, which will run until 2027, with an annual budget of €2 million. The application window for the fifth round of funding closed on 2 June 2026. Assessments of the applications have taken place, and the approved projects for this round will be announced in the near future.
Full details of all funding rounds can be found on the Shared Island Civic Society Fund website: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-foreign-affairs/services/shared-island-civic-society-fund/.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the assessment that has been made of the impact of climate change on global food security; and the role Ireland is playing in international efforts to address this challenge.
reply:
Climate change is a major driver of global food insecurity through its impact on agricultural production, livelihoods, and food prices. The current projections of a strong El Niño weather pattern in 2026 and 2027 have further intensified these pressures, increasing the risk of hunger and food shortages in vulnerable regions. El Niño is expected to significantly worsen global food security by disrupting rainfall patterns, increasing the frequency of droughts, floods, heatwaves and storms, and reducing agricultural production in many regions.
This situation is compounded by the ongoing conflict affecting Black Sea trade routes, and continued instability around the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. The current situation combines disruptions to trade and transport with rising risks to production, severely testing market resilience. This is already affecting vulnerable populations. According to the World Food Programme, an estimated 266 million people were already experiencing acute food insecurity in 2025.
For years, Ireland has been a leader in global efforts to tackle food insecurity and malnutrition. We have been raising the current situation internationally, including during my engagements at he United Nations General Assembly in New York last week. We are also providing significant support to international development and humanitarian organisations, including through our child wasting programme, focused on acute child malnutrition in Africa. question: Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if she plans to revisit the advice of the Attorney General in regard to the Israeli Settlements in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (Prohibition of Importation of Goods) Bill 2026, following the UK government's decision to sanction both goods and services.
reply:

The Act fulfils the commitment set out in the Programme for Government.

It is important to note that some of the proposed measures are being taken by countries that are not members of the EU or of the Customs Union, and that other proposals are still in draft form.
In addition to the legislation we have enacted at the national level, the Government remains focused on progressing action at the EU level to prohibit all trade with Israeli settlements. question: Deputy Conor D. McGuinness asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade for an update on the Government’s position on the United States's embargo against Cuba; the representations made by Ireland through the European Union, the United Nations and in the most recent bilateral engagements with US officials in the past two months.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 56 and 60 together.
Ireland’s position on the embargo imposed by the United States on Cuba is long-standing and clear. Restricting the flow of basic goods, and particularly fuel, to Cuba heightens the suffering of ordinary Cubans. It is Ireland’s position that the US economic embargo serves no constructive purpose, and has impacted negatively on the people of Cuba.
Ireland has consistently voted for UN resolutions calling for the ending of the embargo at the UN General Assembly. Along with the majority of EU Member States, we most recently voted in favour of this annual UN Resolution when it was debated in October 2025.

Ireland has also opposed the inclusion of Cuba on the United States’ list of State Sponsors of Terrorism and the associated measures.

This follows €4 million in EU funding approved as a regional allocation for the Caribbean, which was primarily allocated to the response in Cuba. In 2025, almost €6 million was provided for disaster preparedness and emergency response in Cuba.

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if she accepts the important role that embassies abroad play for Irish citizens in visa application processes and what measures are being taken by her Department to improve response times and customer service standards across the diplomatic and visa systems.
reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, responsibility for matters related to immigration to the State, including visa policy, lies with the Minster for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration.
However, my Department does provide a visa service through its Embassy and broader diplomatic network in a number of countries, under the guidance of the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, where that department does not have a dedicated visa office.
My Department has a limited decision-making role, and can decide on and issue certain categories of visa. These are primarily short stay visa applications and, in some cases, long stay study visas. The Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration decides on visa applications outside these categories, and on visa appeals.
I can assure the Deputy that I recognise the importance of this role, including in promoting Ireland as a place to invest, work, study and visit, and in the implementation of a strategic migration approach, in line with the Programme for Government.
In 2025, Irish Embassies received approximately 66,000 visa applications. In general and across most visa categories, visa processing takes between eight and 12 weeks. However, timelines can vary by location.
I would please refer the Deputy to the relevant Irish Embassy or Consulate webpages for information on average processing times for a specific country.

question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade whether she is aware that organisers of the latest Freedom Flotilla to Gaza have been imprisoned in Tunisia (details supplied); and whether she will make representations to the ambassador and government of Tunisia calling for their release.
reply:

My Department, through our officials in headquarters and in our Embassy in Rabat, which is accredited concurrently to Tunisia, will continue to monitor this situation.

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if Ireland is advancing proposals for the reform of United Nations structures.
reply:
Ireland supports the ongoing UN80 reform initiative launched by UN Secretary-General Guterres in 2025. The initiative aims to strengthen the effectiveness, accountability and representativeness of the UN system amid shrinking resources and rising needs.
Ireland believes that any reforms must serve to strengthen and protect the United Nations' capacity to deliver across the three pillars of Peace and Security, Sustainable Development, and Human Rights, while remaining firmly grounded in the principles of the UN Charter.
Together with our EU partners, Ireland continues to engage actively across all three work-streams of UN80. This includes initiatives to strengthen coordination, coherence and delivery across the UN, via reforms of programmes and structures.
Ireland also continues to advocate for institutional reforms, including reform of the UN Security Council. Ireland has consistently called for the veto power held by the Permanent Five members of the Security Council to be abolished. Ireland has also been clear that Council reform must address the unjust under-representation of Africa and other under-represented regions on the Council and safeguard the right of small states, including Small Island Developing States, to serve on the Council.
My Department will continue to engage on the UN80 process to ensure that Ireland's values and interests are protected and advanced.

question: Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if the Government will be maintaining or increasing current levels of foreign aid funding in budget 2027.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 52 and 80 together.
The Government remains committed to the UN target to provide 0.7% of Gross National Income (GNI) in Official Development Assistance (ODA). This commitment was reaffirmed in A Better World, Ireland's International Development Policy and in the Programme for Government, which commits to increases in ODA, towards the 0.7% target.
Ireland’s total ODA amounted to €1.88 billion in 2025, representing 0.44% of GNI. In recent years, the Government has consistently increased the allocation for the Irish Aid programme managed by the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, which works to address the needs of some of the world’s poorest or most climate-exposed countries and communities and those living in areas affected by conflict.
Budget 2026 provided an allocation of over €840 million for the Irish Aid programme. This was the highest ever allocation in the programme's 52-year history.
Ahead of Budget 2027, I an working to ensure an ODA allocation for the programme in 2027 which continues to deliver on Ireland’s commitment to reaching the furthest behind first. I am also working through our EU Presidency to facilitate discussions at political level on the European Union's continuing commitment to development cooperation, including at the forthcoming informal meeting of EU Development Ministers in Dublin on 8-9 October.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the steps her Department is taking to support the work of the International Criminal Court and to oppose the sanctions currently being imposed on judges and prosecutors in the ICC by the United States.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 38 and 51 together.
Ireland is a strong supporter of the International Criminal Court (ICC), which we view as the cornerstone of the international system of criminal justice. I deeply regret the imposition of US sanctions against thirteen officials of the ICC. Such measures threaten to corrode the international legal order on which all states – but particularly small states like Ireland – depend.
I am aware of ongoing reports that the United States is considering sanctioning the ICC as an institution, which would very significantly impede the operational capacity of the Court. The ICC must be allowed to continue its important work, independently and impartially.
Ireland has been consistent in calling for all measures against the ICC to be withdrawn. The Taoiseach reiterated this principled position during his address to the UN General Assembly during UN High Level Week on 24 September.
The Government believes that a coordinated EU response is the most effective way to protect the ICC and its officials. In our role as President of the EU Council, Ireland is committed to playing its part in maintaining full solidarity with the Court at this crucial moment.

question: Deputy Donnchadh Ó Laoghaire asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade her position on the banning of political parties by Israel's central elections committee ahead of elections there next month.
reply:
I am concerned that Israel's Central Elections Committee voted to disqualify the two Arab-majority lists contesting the upcoming parliamentary elections in Israel. If this decision is not overturned, it would exclude Arab-majority parties contesting the elections. I note that the Committee also voted to disqualify two individual candidates standing for those parties.
It is essential that the elections, scheduled to take on Tuesday, 27 October, are held in a free, fair and inclusive context. Arab citizens of Israel make up approximately twenty percent of Israel’s population.
I note that the decision of the Central Elections Committee is subject to review by the Israeli Supreme Court. In past elections, the Israeli Supreme Court has consistently overturned attempts to disqualify Arab-majority parties, citing a commitment to protecting democratic franchise and freedom of speech.

question: Deputy Tony McCormack asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the measures being taken through Ireland’s diplomatic network and international trade engagement to promote and diversify overseas market opportunities for Irish agricultural and agrifood exports.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 25, 41 and 49 together.
This Government is committed to support Irish companies with their market diversification ambitions. Market diversification protects against sudden changes in the global economy, opens new trading opportunities and enhances economic resilience.
The Action Plan on Market Diversification is part of a comprehensive response by the Government to recent changes in the global trading environment. The Plan was developed jointly by my Department and the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment with input from other Government Departments and Agencies. Both Departments drive implementation of the Action Plan through the Headquarters Market Team (HQMT), which is co-chaired by senior officials from both Departments. The HQMT also includes senior representatives from Department and State agencies engaged in promoting Ireland internationally.
The first implementation progress report was published in March and showed strong implementation. A second implementation will be published by the end of the year. The momentum has continued throughout 2026. Some of the early measures worth noting are the increased people resources put in place by the State Agencies in diverse locations including Korea, UAE, India and New Zealand as well as new market diversification attaches from my Department in our consulates in Atlanta, Austin, New York, Chicago and Los Angeles.

question: Deputy Shay Brennan asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade her response to the recent attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 47 and 90 together.
The Government has strongly condemned Russia’s attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport in August.
This activity is part of a clear trend. It forms part of a broader, coordinated, and long-standing hybrid campaign aimed at threatening and undermining the security, resilience and democratic foundations of the EU, its Member States and its partners.
In response to the Leipzig incident, I expressed my full solidarity with Germany, and with all Member States affected by Russia’s reckless and increasingly frequent hybrid attacks. I discussed the issue with the HRVP, Kaja Kallas, and my German and other EU counterparts at the meeting of EU Foreign Ministers I hosted in Druid's Glen in early September.
The Ambassador of the Russian Federation was summoned by senior officials of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade on 3 September to hear expression of Ireland’s strong condemnation. Many of our EU partners also did so. Russia’s attempts to divide us and to weaken our support for Ukraine will not succeed.
Ireland is extremely concerned at the continued increased in hybrid activity. Russia’s actions threaten the security of EU citizens, as well as regional stability and international peace.
We support the full use of all tools available to prevent, deter, and respond to Russia’s hybrid activities, including through sanctions.
As Presidency, we are working closely with EU partners to navigate our complex and evolving threat env

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the actions she intends to take to raise the recent crackdown on LGBTQ+ activists in the Republic of Türkiye.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 29, 46 and 75 together.
I am deeply concerned about recent measures, including legal proceedings and arrests, against LGBTIQ+ organisations and persons in Türkiye. As an EU candidate country, member of the Council of Europe, and a party to international human rights instruments, Türkiye is expected to uphold the highest democratic standards and to ensure the respect of fundamental rights for all, including for LGBTIQ+ persons.
Every person, regardless of sexual orientation, gender identity, or any other characteristic, is entitled to equality, dignity and the full enjoyment of their human rights. The promotion and protection of the rights of LGBTIQ+ persons is a domestic and foreign policy priority for Ireland, and this is reflected in our campaign for membership of the UN Human Rights Council, where defending the rights of LGBTIQ+ persons is one of our five thematic priorities.
Ireland continues to support initiatives in the EU and other international fora which promote and protect the rights of LGBTIQ+ people, and which condemn violence and discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Ireland stands in full solidarity with LGBTIQ+ persons and their allies in Türkiye. As part of ongoing bilateral engagement, Ireland raises human rights issues, including regarding LGBTIQ+ persons, with the Turkish authorities.
Ireland fully supports the statement of 18 September by the European External Action Service expressing concer

question: Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade when the next meeting of the EU General Affairs Council will take place; and the likely agenda for the meeting.
reply:
The General Affairs Council (GAC) will next meet on 13 October in Luxembourg. The Minister for European Affairs and Defence, Thomas Byrne TD, will chair the meeting as Presidency. The October Council meeting will also build on progress made at both the informal GAC in Dublin on 3-4 September as well as the GAC in Brussels on 22 September.
Topics on the agenda in October include an update on the simplification agenda and the joint declaration on the legislative priorities for 2027 and the One Europe, One Market Roadmap. GAC Ministers will hold a discussion on the state of play on the rule of law in Hungary and are expected to approve Council conclusions on the importance of inclusive democratic participation. The GAC will also prepare the meeting of the EU leaders at the European Council (15-16 October) which will look at competitiveness, Ukraine, the Middle East, security and defence, the MFF and enlargement and reforms.
The Presidency will also host an event on the margins of the GAC in October to mark the accession of candidate countries to the European Centre for Democratic Resilience.
On the enlargement side, the Presidency would hope to hold a number of Intergovernmental Councils (IGCs) on the margins of this meeting to make progress on the accession process of candidate countries.
A key issue for the GAC in October will be the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) 2028-2034. The Presidency continues to advance negotiations on the MFF so that Leaders can reach agree

question: Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade to provide an update on efforts to increase aid supplies crossing the border into Gaza.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 14, 31 and 44 together.
Ireland continues to use every opportunity at the EU level and internationally to stress our grave concerns about the catastrophic humanitarian situation in Gaza, and ongoing Israeli operations in both Gaza and the West Bank. During Ireland’s Presidency of the Council of the EU, we are working to maintain this focus at EU level. The situation in Gaza and the West Bank was discussed at the Informal Meeting of EU Foreign Ministers that I hosted in Wicklow last month. Ireland continues to press for appropriate EU action in response to egregious Israeli breaches of international law, human rights and democratic principles.
The situation in Palestine was a central focus of my engagement with EU and other international partners during High Level Week at the UN last week. Ireland participated in a number of events focused on Israel and Palestine, including the meeting jointly organised by France, the UK and Canada one year on from the New York Declaration. I attended the High-Level meeting of the Global Alliance for the Implementation of the Two State Solution, as well as a High Level event on International Humanitarian Law.
At the Global Alliance meeting, I reiterated Ireland's concern about the appalling situation for people in Gaza, who continue to endure intolerable hardships. question: Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade to provide a report from the UN General Assembly.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 43 and 61 together.
I attended the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly last week in New York. Ireland's delegation was led by an Taoiseach and also included my colleague, Neale Richmond, TD, Minister of State for International Development and Diaspora. High-Level Week provides an important opportunity to advance Ireland's foreign policy priorities through participation in high-level events and engagement with a wide range of interlocutors.
This year, reflecting many of our EU Presidency priorities, our focus was on support for multilateralism and the international legal order, addressing the conflicts in Ukraine, the Middle East, and Sudan, Ireland's long-standing commitment to human rights and accountability, including in the context of our candidacy for the Human Rights Council for the 2027-2029 term, and on highlighting Ireland's support for the Sustainable Development Goals and humanitarian action.
To begin the week, I co-hosted an event with Nobel Laureate Malala Yousafza on the situation of women and girls in Afghanistan five years after the Taliban takeover. This event called on the international community to take action to end the systematic exclusion of women and girls from public life and to address the profound human rights and humanitarian crises in Afghanistan. question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the number of times she has met with the Israeli Ambassador to Ireland in the past 12 months.
reply:
Ireland continues to maintain diplomatic channels of communication with Israel, following the decision of the government of Israel in December 2024 to close its embassy in Dublin. Our embassy in Israel continues to carry out important work.
The Ambassador of Israel to Ireland, Her Excellency Ms Dana Erlich, is accredited to Ireland on a non-resident basis. I have not met with her in the past 12 months.

question: Deputy Tony McCormack asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade to provide an update on the Department’s role in implementing the Government Action Plan on Market Diversification; and the measures being taken through Ireland’s diplomatic network to support Irish SMEs and indigenous businesses seeking to access new export markets.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 25, 41 and 49 together.
This Government is committed to support Irish companies with their market diversification ambitions. Market diversification protects against sudden changes in the global economy, opens new trading opportunities and enhances economic resilience.
The Action Plan on Market Diversification is part of a comprehensive response by the Government to recent changes in the global trading environment. The Plan was developed jointly by my Department and the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment with input from other Government Departments and Agencies. Both Departments drive implementation of the Action Plan through the Headquarters Market Team (HQMT), which is co-chaired by senior officials from both Departments. The HQMT also includes senior representatives from Department and State agencies engaged in promoting Ireland internationally.
The first implementation progress report was published in March and showed strong implementation. A second implementation will be published by the end of the year. The momentum has continued throughout 2026. Some of the early measures worth noting are the increased people resources put in place by the State Agencies in diverse locations including Korea, UAE, India and New Zealand as well as new market diversification attaches from my Department in our consulates in Atlanta, Austin, New York, Chicago and Los Angeles.

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade her views that there are infringements on the right to protest in Germany in relation to the right of people to protest in solidarity with the Palestinian people.
reply:
The promotion and protection of human rights, including the rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly, are vital elements of Ireland’s foreign policy. Ireland consistently advocates for the protection of these rights internationally and encourages all States to uphold their obligations under international human rights law.
These principles guide all of our engagements with Germany.
Germany is a democratic constitutional state governed by the rule of law, where state authority is bound by the constitution, the law, and the justice system. Fundamental rights are protected through the German constitution as well as through Germany’s obligations under the European Convention on Human Rights, the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights and other international instruments.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade whether she has advocated for the use of the EU blocking mechanism to protect US citizens in Europe facing sanctions from the Trump administration.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 38 and 51 together.
Ireland is a strong supporter of the International Criminal Court (ICC), which we view as the cornerstone of the international system of criminal justice. I deeply regret the imposition of US sanctions against thirteen officials of the ICC. Such measures threaten to corrode the international legal order on which all states – but particularly small states like Ireland – depend.
I am aware of ongoing reports that the United States is considering sanctioning the ICC as an institution, which would very significantly impede the operational capacity of the Court. The ICC must be allowed to continue its important work, independently and impartially.
Ireland has been consistent in calling for all measures against the ICC to be withdrawn. The Taoiseach reiterated this principled position during his address to the UN General Assembly during UN High Level Week on 24 September.
The Government believes that a coordinated EU response is the most effective way to protect the ICC and its officials. In our role as President of the EU Council, Ireland is committed to playing its part in maintaining full solidarity with the Court at this crucial moment.

question: Deputy Rose Conway-Walsh asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if her Department has begun any internal planning concerning future constitutional change.
reply:
The Programme for Government states clearly that this Government is committed to the unity of the Irish people. This can only be achieved through a sustained focus on and investment in reconciliation. We remain steadfast in implementing the Good Friday Agreement in full and supporting the function of all of its institutions.
Our commitment is backed by our Shared Island Initiative, to which we have allocated €2 billion through to 2035.
The Initiative is enabling the largest-ever programme of all-island investment across all sectors, to build a more connected island, in terms of infrastructure, services, our economy and, crucially, between people.
The Shared Island Initiative is just one part of our work to promote peace and reconciliation on this island, work that also includes my Department's Reconciliation Fund, which awards grants to organisations working to build better relations within and between traditions in Northern Ireland, between North and South, and between Ireland and Britain. My Department also supports and provides the Dublin Secretariat for the International Fund for Ireland which continues to do important work in Northern Ireland and the border counties.
The Government is working to build a more prosperous and reconciled island for people North and South, and in the event of a future referendum, we will make all necessary preparations, in accordance with the terms of the Constitution and the principles and procedures of the Agreement.

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade her views on the need to block trade with illegal settlements in the Palestinian West Bank; her views on the need to freeze assets of companies who support the genocide in Gaza; and to sanction members of the IDF and Israeli Ministers.
reply:
The Israeli Settlements in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (Prohibition of Importation of Goods) Act came into effect on 15 September. The importation of goods originating in Israeli settlements into Ireland is now an offence under section 14 of the Customs Act 2015. The Act fulfils the commitment set out in the Programme for Government.
The Act will contribute positively to Ireland’s efforts to uphold and comply with international law, including the findings of the 2024 ICJ Advisory Opinion, as well as contributing positively to Irish and international efforts to prevent unilateral actions that impinge upon the right of the Palestinian people to self-determination, and upon the viability of the two-State solution.
In addition to the legislation we have enacted at the national level, the Government remains focused on progressing action at the EU level to prohibit all trade with Israeli settlements. Collective EU action will have greater impact than any measures adopted by an individual Member State and is the strongest and most effective route to ensure EU compliance with international law, as I have set out in detail on a number of previous occasions.
The Government supports targeted sanctions against Israeli individuals and entities and has consistently called for appropriate action at EU level in response to egregious Israeli breaches of human rights and democratic principles.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the funding schemes that may be available to support restoration works at the historic boundary wall at Seir Kieran Cemetery, Clareen, Birr, County Offaly; and whether projects of this nature would be eligible for consideration under the built heritage investment scheme, and the historic structures fund or any other relevant heritage conservation programmes.
reply:
The Community Monuments Fund (CMF) is administered by my Department through the Local Authorities and the call for applications for the 2027 scheme will be announced in the coming weeks.
The Community Monuments Fund provides funding for projects in relation to:
(i) Archaeological Monuments that are included in the Record of Monuments and Places (RMP) under the National Monuments Act 1930 (as amended);
(ii) Archaeological Monuments that are identified in the Sites and Monuments Record compiled by the National Monuments Service.
The Built Heritage Investment Scheme (BHIS) and the Historic Structures Fund (HSF) are administered by my Department through the Local Authorities and both schemes are currently open. For BHIS, applications must be submitted to the Local Authority no later than 30 October 2026. For HSF, applications must be submitted to the Local Authority no later than 27 November 2026.
Full details about eligibility for both schemes may be found on gov.ie at www.gov.ie/en/department-of-housing-local-government-and-heritage/services/built-heritage-investment-scheme-bhis/ and www.gov.ie/en/department-of-housing-local-government-and-heritage/services/historic-structures-fund/.
For applications to all of these schemes it is highly advisable to make contact with The Heritage Officer in the relevant Local Authority.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to provide an update on the commitment to introduce solar planning guidelines in the Programme for Government; the timeline for delivery; if guidelines will be delivered by the end of 2026.
reply:
In line with commitments in the Programme for Government 2025, my Department is working with the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment (DCEE), which holds policy responsibility for renewable energy matters, in respect of the introduction of a number of National Planning Statements related to Ireland's Climate Action Plan target to increase the share of electricity generated from renewable sources up to 80% in 2030. This includes the preparation of a National Planning Statement for solar energy development.
Further to the commencement of Chapter 3 of Part 3 of the Planning and Development Act 2024 on 2 October 2025, provisions for National Planning Statements have been introduced to replace the provisions for Ministerial guidelines issued under section 28 of the Planning and Development Act 2000. All existing Section 28 guidelines will, over time, be revoked and replaced with new National Planning Statements. Any current section 28 guidelines will however remain in force until revoked or replaced by a corresponding National Planning Statement. The timing of the issuing of National Planning Statements will be based on Government priorities.

question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number of social homes retrofitted to date and the number he expects to be retrofitted by 2030.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 178 and 344 together.
Since 2013, my Department’s Energy Efficiency Retrofit Programme (EERP) has supported the retrofit of 85,292 local authority owned social homes requiring insulation and energy efficiency upgrades, with more than €0.5 billion provided to local authorities to support these works in the period to end-2025.
A revised EERP, introduced in 2021, is targeting the retrofit 36,500 local authority homes by 2030 to a post works BER equivalent of the previous B2 standard (125 kWh/m²/year). Eligible works include insulation upgrades, replacement of windows and doors, heat pump installation and associated works. Since 2021, over 11,000 social homes have been upgraded, supported by more than €342 million provided by my Department in the period.
Some €140 million has been allocated to local authorities under the EERP this year. This represents an increase of more than 50% on the previous year's allocation and is expected to facilitate the retrofit of approximately 3,500 social homes.
A year-by-year breakdown of funding and completed retrofits for 2013-2025 is available on my Department’s website at: www.gov.ie/en/publication/668c1-energy-efficiency-retrofitting-programme-expenditure-output/
Details of the Midlands Energy Retrofit Pilot Programme are available at: www.gov.ie/en/publication/b86b3-midlands-energy-retrofit-programme-expenditure-and-units/#
Data on the number of retrofits completed by local authorities in 2026 will be publishe

question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether he has engaged with local authorities on rates schemes for vacant buildings to encourage new enterprise.
reply:
Local authorities have been levying and collecting rates under the Local Government Rates and Other Matters Act 2019 since 1 January 2024. The Act expanded the range of measures available to local authorities to support local businesses and address specific local economic challenges.
Section 9 of the Act provides for the introduction of rates vacancy abatement schemes. These schemes afford local authorities considerable flexibility in developing targeted interventions for vacant commercial properties. In determining the design of such schemes, local authorities may take account of local economic conditions, the extent and nature of commercial vacancy, and wider regeneration objectives. Vacancy abatement schemes may be tailored to particular towns, geographic areas, classes of property or categories of ratepayer. The introduction and operation of any such scheme is a matter for the elected members of the local authority.
Section 15 of the Act enables local authorities to make rates waiver schemes in support of local and national policy objectives. This provision further enhances the capacity of local authorities and elected members to respond to the particular needs and challenges of their areas.
A waiver scheme may be introduced where it supports the implementation of:
• the National Planning Framework;
• a local area plan;
• a local economic and community plan; or
• an urban area plan, priority area plan or coordinated area plan.

question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage for an update on the role his Department is taking in the Butter Exchange Project in Cork city.
reply:
THRIVE (Town Centre First Heritage Revival) Scheme is a grant scheme of c. €120million for local authorities which is co-funded by the Government and the European Union and delivered under Ireland’s two ERDF (European Regional Development Fund) Regional Programmes. The THRIVE Scheme provides funding for the preparation of Town Centre First Plans, strategies and project development work in towns to enable future capital funding applications to be made to Government for the identified projects in these plans. THRIVE also supports town regeneration through direct capital funding of €115 million in total for the implementation of identified heritage-related projects in town centres – with 19 projects currently being funded across the country.
The Shandon Exchange, located in Shandon, Cork City, comprises of the Butter Exchange Building and the adjacent Weighmaster’s House which have been derelict for a number of years. Both properties will be regenerated to ensure the conservation and future safeguarding of the building complex. Cork City Council forecast a total project cost of €11.5 million. €7m of this will be funded by the THRIVE award and €4.5 million will be funded by Cork City Council.
Further Details are available here: www.corkcity.ie/en/council-services/services/planning/thrive/.

question: Deputy Micheál Carrigy asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the specific timeline for the notification of successful applicants under the basic income for the arts (2026–2029) scheme, which closed for applications on 12 May 2026; the exact date when applicants will be informed of the selection outcome; the precise date when the first backdated weekly payments of €325 will reach the accounts of successful recipients.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 300, 301, 303, 304, 305, 306, 307, 309, 310, 311, 312, 313, 314, 315, 316, 319, 321, 322, 323, 324, 326, 327, 328, 329, 331, 332, 333, 334, 335, 336, 337, 338, 339, 340 and 341 together.
In February this year I announced that the Government had approved a permanent successor to the Basic Income for the Arts pilot scheme and that 2,000 artists would be provided with funding of €325 per week for three years. This is a major milestone for the arts in Ireland and I am particularly pleased that the research my Department conducted provided Government with a clear evidence base upon which to make that decision.
The deadline for application to the Basic Income for the Arts 2026 - 2029 was 5pm on Tuesday 12th May, with over 10,000 applications received by the deadline.
Like the pilot scheme selection is via an anonymous random selection process, this is considered the fairest method where there is not enough funding for all eligible applicants. The selection process took place in May with independent oversight by EY. The selection ranked all applications from 1 - 10,000 and eligibility checks then started from the first selected applicant to determine if those selected were eligible. That assessment process is ongoing to determine the final 2,000 applicants who will receive the BIA.
I appreciate that applicants are eager to know the outcome, however, in order to protect the integrity of the scheme the assessment process is by necessity very intensive

question: Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade for an update on Ireland's EU Presidency; and the way in which Irish priorities are being advanced.
reply:
Ireland assumed the Presidency of the Council of the European Union on 1 July and will hold this role until 31 December 2026. Since the start of our term, we have made substantial progress in advancing policy objectives across our three core priorities of competitiveness, values and security.
Early achievements include renewed momentum on EU enlargement, including chairing the largest number of accession conferences held in a single day in over twenty years. We secured agreement on further packages of sanctions against Russia, and the extension of temporary protection for those fleeing Ukraine. We have made important progress on measures to better protect children from sexual abuse online. We are advancing significant measures aimed at strengthening Europe’s competitiveness.
That means making it easier for Irish and European businesses to grow, invest and create jobs. We are committed to protecting children online, supporting our farmers and rural communities, strengthening Europe’s security and standing firmly with Ukraine. And we are making every effort to ensure that the European Union remains competitive in a rapidly changing global economy.
We are delivering a successful programme of Presidency meetings, both in Brussels and here in Ireland, which has helped to strengthen relationships and to move our agenda forward.

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport to provide a breakdown of successful school-related applications under the three most recent completed rounds of the CSFF and its predecessor, the Sports Capital & Equipment Programme, specifying the school, county, partner sports club or organisation, project description, amount allocated and amount drawn down; the requirements for schools applying under the forthcoming round, including joint applications, facility-sharing agreements and community access; and whether his Department provides school-specific guidance or case studies of successful applications, in tabular form.
reply:
The provision of sports facilities in school settings is primarily the responsibility of the Minister for Education and Youth and the school governing authorities.
The information requested encompasses multiple rounds of the Community Sport Facilities Fund (CSFF) and is presently being collated by my Department. A report will be forwarded directly to the Deputy as soon as it is finalised. Details of all CSFF allocations are available on the Department's website at www.gov.ie/en/department-of-culture-communications-and-sport/collections/sports-capital-programme-allocations/.
I have also recently met with officials from the Department of Education and Youth to discuss how the benefits for sporting organisations and schools from working together on CSFF applications can be optimised and there has been subsequent further engagement between officials from both Departments.
A new online grant management system for CSFF, SPRAOI, went live on Monday 28 September for registrations; any clubs or organisations that are not already registered with the Department may do so now.
The window for funding applications will run from Monday 19 October 2026 to Friday 26 February 2027.

question: Deputy Donnchadh Ó Laoghaire asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade for an update on her Department's recent engagements with the Government of Ukraine in relation to the ongoing conflict.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 30 and 32 together.
Ireland’s support to Ukraine is unwavering and remains a key focus of my engagements with my EU counterparts, both bilaterally and in Brussels. This war and the threat posed by Russia is not only an existential issue for Ukraine but is a major challenge to the security of Europe.
During our EU Presidency, Ireland is working with our EU and international partners in support of Ukraine and efforts to secure a just, comprehensive and lasting peace.
We were honoured to host President Zelenskyy in Ireland on the first day of our Presidency. The Taoiseach visited Kyiv on 23 July to express Ireland’s continued support for Ukraine.
Russia’s aggression features prominently at each meeting of the Foreign Affairs Council. Ukraine was a key focus of the first meeting of our Presidency on 13 July, including an event I co-hosted with the High Representative to focus on civilian detainees in Ukraine’s occupied territories.
During this event, EU foreign ministers held an informal exchange over breakfast with Ukraine’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Andrii Sybiha, as well as representatives of two Ukrainian human rights organisations that focus on the issue.
The Council then discussed Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, following an initial address by Minister Sybiha, who gave an overview of the situation on the ground and Ukraine’s most urgent needs.
The ensuing ministerial discussions focused on Ukraine's energy preparedness ahead

I propose to take Questions Nos. 300, 301, 303, 304, 305, 306, 307, 309, 310, 311, 312, 313, 314, 315, 316, 319, 321, 322, 323, 324, 326, 327, 328, 329, 331, 332, 333, 334, 335, 336, 337, 338, 339, 340 and 341 together.
In February this year I announced that the Government had approved a permanent successor to the Basic Income for the Arts pilot scheme and that 2,000 artists would be provided with funding of €325 per week for three years. This is a major milestone for the arts in Ireland and I am particularly pleased that the research my Department conducted provided Government with a clear evidence base upon which to make that decision.
The deadline for application to the Basic Income for the Arts 2026 - 2029 was 5pm on Tuesday 12th May, with over 10,000 applications received by the deadline.
Like the pilot scheme selection is via an anonymous random selection process, this is considered the fairest method where there is not enough funding for all eligible applicants. The selection process took place in May with independent oversight by EY. The selection ranked all applications from 1 - 10,000 and eligibility checks then started from the first selected applicant to determine if those selected were eligible. That assessment process is ongoing to determine the final 2,000 applicants who will receive the BIA.
I appreciate that applicants are eager to know the outcome, however, in order to protect the integrity of the scheme the assessment process is by necessity very intensive

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade given that Ireland has presidency of the EU, if she will do everything possible to end the conflict and genocide in Gaza.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 14, 31 and 44 together.
Ireland continues to use every opportunity at the EU level and internationally to stress our grave concerns about the catastrophic humanitarian situation in Gaza, and ongoing Israeli operations in both Gaza and the West Bank. During Ireland’s Presidency of the Council of the EU, we are working to maintain this focus at EU level. The situation in Gaza and the West Bank was discussed at the Informal Meeting of EU Foreign Ministers that I hosted in Wicklow last month. Ireland continues to press for appropriate EU action in response to egregious Israeli breaches of international law, human rights and democratic principles.

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport to confirm specifically that the Kingston Park and Millers Lane application remains eligible for consideration from additional funding under the 2024 LSSIF round; to confirm its status on his Department's reserve list; and whether the granting of full planning approval by An Coimisiún Pleanála will now be reflected in his Department's assessment of the project's readiness and deliverability.
reply:
The Large-Scale Sports Infrastructure Fund (LSSIF) was established under the National Sports Policy to provide Exchequer support for larger sports facility projects, typically those requiring investments greater than the maximum available under the Community Sport Facilities Fund (CSFF).
The 2024 round of LSSIF received an unprecedented demand for funding, amounting to €665 million from 96 applicants. As a result of this significant demand, a range of valid applications, including the application referred to by the Deputy, did not receive an LSSIF allocation at the allocation stage.
It should be noted that, should additional funding become available, eligible applications that did not receive funding under the 2024 round and whose proposed projects align with key strategic national priorities and strategies such as the National Swimming Strategy could be considered for funding support in advance of a future round of the LSSIF.
With regard to a future round of the LSSIF, my current focus is on ensuring project delivery under the first two rounds of the LSSIF, 2018 and 2024, and this process will inform any decisions regarding the timing of the next round of LSSIF funding.
