question: Deputy Shay Brennan asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade for a report on the discussions on Ukraine at the most recent EU Foreign Affairs council.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 30 and 32 together.
Ireland’s support to Ukraine is unwavering and remains a key focus of my engagements with my EU counterparts, both bilaterally and in Brussels. This war and the threat posed by Russia is not only an existential issue for Ukraine but is a major challenge to the security of Europe.
During our EU Presidency, Ireland is working with our EU and international partners in support of Ukraine and efforts to secure a just, comprehensive and lasting peace.
We were honoured to host President Zelenskyy in Ireland on the first day of our Presidency. The Taoiseach visited Kyiv on 23 July to express Ireland’s continued support for Ukraine.
Russia’s aggression features prominently at each meeting of the Foreign Affairs Council. Ukraine was a key focus of the first meeting of our Presidency on 13 July, including an event I co-hosted with the High Representative to focus on civilian detainees in Ukraine’s occupied territories.
During this event, EU foreign ministers held an informal exchange over breakfast with Ukraine’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Andrii Sybiha, as well as representatives of two Ukrainian human rights organisations that focus on the issue.
The Council then discussed Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, following an initial address by Minister Sybiha, who gave an overview of the situation on the ground and Ukraine’s most urgent needs.
The ensuing ministerial discussions focused on Ukraine's energy preparedness ahead

question: Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if there are circumstances when a club (details supplied) can qualify for tier 2 CCSF funding; and if this element is reserved for regional applications.
reply:
My Department is currently preparing for the next round of the Community Sport Facilities Fund (CSFF), which I expect to open soon. A new online grant management system for CSFF, SPRAOI, went live on Monday 28 September for registrations. Any clubs or organisations that are not already registered with the Department may do so from that date.
The Department has collated extensive feedback from sporting clubs and organisations as an input to the key changes in the new 2026 round. The terms and conditions for the next CSFF round, and the timing of the application window, can be found on the Department's website. Regional Tier 2 Grant funding is only available to Local authorities and NGBs.
A wide reaching information campaign will be undertaken to assist clubs in any queries that have in relation to the application. The 2026 round will prioritise areas and sports that have been under-invested in over the years.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her attention has been drawn to concerns raised by PME students in relation to the structuring of their course and confusion related to qualifying modules (details supplied).
reply:
The Teaching Council is the body with the statutory authority and responsibility for the regulation of the teaching profession in Ireland including the registration of teachers in the State.
The Teaching Council registers teachers under the Teaching Council Act 2001-2015 (www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2001/act/8/enacted/en/htm) and in line with the Teaching Council Registration Regulations, 2025 (www.teachingcouncil.ie/assets/uploads/2025/10/SI.2025.0482_TC_Registration_Regulations.pdf). As set out in the Schedule of the Regulations, the Council registers teachers under five routes of registration: Route 1 - Primary, Route 2 - Post-primary, Route 3 - Further Education, Route 4 - Other and Route 5 - Student Teacher. The qualification requirements for each route are set down in the Schedule. My department has no role in the registration of individual teachers.
It is the Council’s responsibility to ensure that all teachers entering the profession in Ireland have met the required standards. These standards have been established following extensive consultation with relevant stakeholders, research, and in accordance with Department of Education and Youth's policies and priorities and developed over a number of years.
There is a curricular subject requirement (CSR) for registration under ‘Route 2: Post-primary’ which falls under the Teaching Council’s statutory functions set out in Section 31(5) of the Teaching Council Act 2001 and Route 2 of the Teaching Council [Registration] Regul

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Education and Youth the supports available for the installation of electric vehicle charging points at schools.
reply:
My Departments Climate Action Summer Works Scheme (CASWS) provides funding to schools for the provision of Electric Vehicle Chargers.
In March 2025, my Department announced the roll out of a new Climate Action Summer Works Scheme (CASWS). The CASWS (which was previously named the Summer Works Scheme) placed a strong emphasis on sustainability. Schools can now undertake additional measures such as insulation upgrades, LED lighting installation, EV charger provision, bike rack facilities to support active travel and other climate-focused works alongside traditional maintenance.
The CASWS enables individual school authorities to undertake small-scale building works on a devolved basis that, ideally, can be carried out during the summer months or at other times that avoid disrupting the operation of the school. The CASWS operates on a multi-annual basis across a number of categories of works.
The scheme opened for applications on the 1st May and the application window closed on the 30th of June 2025, with over 1400 applications being received. In November 2025, my Department announced the first tranche of approvals under the new Climate Action Summer Works Scheme. 297 projects were approved to proceed and involve primary, post primary and special schools, along with projects in all counties and across all categories of works.
It is anticipated that the next tranche of approvals will be announced in October 2026.
Full details of the of the announcement and the list of schools appr

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Education and Youth when the tender report supplement for a school building project is expected to be submitted.
reply:
The project referred to by the Deputy is a campus project and is devolved for delivery to Galway and Roscommon Education and Training Board (GRETB).
The approved brief for Gaelscoil Riada provides for a new 16 classroom primary school building including a 2-classroom SEN provision.
The approved brief for Coláiste an Eachraidh provides for a new post primary school building with a long-term projected enrolment of 450 pupils, including a 3-classroom SEN provision.
The project is progressing through the Tender Stage of the architectural design process. A Letter of Intent has been issued and work is ongoing on the preparation of a Tender Report Supplement for submission to the Department. As completion of this work is dependent on a number of elements being finalised by the Design Team, it is not possible to provide a definitive timeline for submission of the report at this stage.
Department officials continue to engage closely with patron bodies, management bodies and schools with respect to the timing of the progression of projects to tender and/or construction over the period 2026 to 2027. This includes continued engagement with GRETB with respect to the progression of this project.
The current status of all projects continues to be set out under item number ten at the following link: www.gov.ie. This is updated on a regular basis to reflect project progress through the various stages of capital appraisal, site acquisition, design, tender and construction.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will address the concerns raised in correspondence (details supplied) regarding the adequacy of special educational and SNA supports for a child with a hearing impairment and additional assessed needs who has recently commenced primary school; and the steps being taken by the NCSE to review the allocation of SNA resources to the school concerned.
reply:
This government is fully committed to supporting students with special educational needs to fulfil their full potential and the Programme for Government makes a number of commitments to deliver on this objective.
The National Council for Special Education (NCSE) is, in the first instance, the primary body responsible for the matter the Deputy has raised. I will arrange for your query to be forwarded to the NCSE for their attention and direct reply. Deputies are also welcome to raise such queries with the NCSE directly through their dedicated Oireachtas email address.
My department and the NCSE are committed to delivering an education system that is of the highest quality and where every child and young person feels valued and is actively supported and nurtured to achieve their full potential.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she will consider ring-fencing €12 million from the recently announced additional €35 million ICT funding allocation for schools to support the replacement and upgrading of computer equipment used for design and communication graphics (DCG) in post-primary schools; if her Department has assessed the adequacy of existing DCG computer infrastructure nationwide.
reply:
As the Deputy is aware, I announced earlier this year €35 million in grant funding for Information and Communications Technology (ICT) with this funding issuing to all recognised primary and post-primary schools in January 2026. This brings the total investment in ICT in schools under this current strategy to €170m.
Under the Education Act, the Boards of Management of Schools have responsibility for the day to day management of schools. Decisions regarding the use and deployment of digital technology in schools is therefore a matter for the Board of Management of each school in the context of their digital learning planning. Schools are advised to consult with members of the school community including parents when planning for the introduction of digital technologies including devices with cost and other implications being fully considered by the Boards of Management before a decision is made.
Schools, in consultation with parents, are responsible for decisions on the use of digital technology, including tablet devices, laptops, and learning platforms, and how best to manage their integration into classroom practice reflective of their own context and requirement. This includes the integration of Design and Computer Graphic`s(DCG) in their school. Once the integration of DCG has happened in schools, it is a matter for the board of management and the schools to include the relevant required upgrades in their Digital Learning Plan and do this in conjunction with the ICT grant.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Education and Youth the number of school placement hours worked by student teachers in the 2025-2026 academic year, broken down by county, in tabular form.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 291 and 292 together.
School placement is a central feature of initial Teacher Education (ITE) Programmes. Student teachers must successfully complete this element of the programme.
School Placement is viewed as teacher education rather than employment. The principal aim and function of school placement is to help the student teacher develop practical skills through observing and reflecting on the professional teacher working with pupils in the classroom. This will enable them to bring together the theoretical and practical elements of the course work with the aim of acquiring practical skills in classroom management, curriculum planning, and the organisation of pupils learning activities.

Céim sets out the requirements that all ITE programmes in Ireland must meet in order to gain accreditation from the Teaching Council. It is also a benchmark for anybody seeking to register as a teacher in Ireland. In line with these revised standards, primary and post primary student teachers must spend between 24 and 30 weeks on school placement as part of their ITE programme.

reply:

Student teachers can make direct contact with the institution that they plan to attend to consider what supports may be available.
Any student experiencing financial hardship can apply to the Student Assistance Fund (SAF) which provides financial support to full or part-time students who are experiencing financial difficulties while attending college. question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if Ireland and its European Union partners will use all possible diplomatic avenues and approaches to address the Republic of Türkiye's persecution of LGBTQ+ persons.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 29, 46 and 75 together.
I am deeply concerned about recent measures, including legal proceedings and arrests, against LGBTIQ+ organisations and persons in Türkiye. As an EU candidate country, member of the Council of Europe, and a party to international human rights instruments, Türkiye is expected to uphold the highest democratic standards and to ensure the respect of fundamental rights for all, including for LGBTIQ+ persons.
Every person, regardless of sexual orientation, gender identity, or any other characteristic, is entitled to equality, dignity and the full enjoyment of their human rights. The promotion and protection of the rights of LGBTIQ+ persons is a domestic and foreign policy priority for Ireland, and this is reflected in our campaign for membership of the UN Human Rights Council, where defending the rights of LGBTIQ+ persons is one of our five thematic priorities.
Ireland continues to support initiatives in the EU and other international fora which promote and protect the rights of LGBTIQ+ people, and which condemn violence and discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Ireland stands in full solidarity with LGBTIQ+ persons and their allies in Türkiye. As part of ongoing bilateral engagement, Ireland raises human rights issues, including regarding LGBTIQ+ persons, with the Turkish authorities.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Education and Youth whether her Department has any plans to review Circular 29/2007, regarding incremental credit; and whether there is a timeline for same.
reply:
The criteria for the award of incremental credit are set out in the Department of Education’s Circulars 29/2007 and 29/2010 for Post-Primary teachers. These circulars provide for the award of incremental credit in respect of prior teaching service, including overseas teaching service, both within and outside the EU and/or relevant non-teaching service.
Teaching service given outside the Republic of Ireland by a qualified teacher in a school or college must be deemed to be equivalent to teaching service given in a primary or post primary school in the Republic of Ireland. This includes teaching service given in a public or private secondary school abroad.
Where a school satisfies the criteria set out in the circulars to have service at that school recognised for incremental credit, an award of incremental credit can be made.
There is no contractual entitlement to incremental credit; applicants must submit a fully completed incremental credit application to have prior service assessed. An award of incremental credit is based on the incremental credit application submitted to either my department or an ETB.
The criteria for the award of incremental credit to recognised teachers were agreed under the auspices of the Teachers Conciliation Council (TCC) and are subject to review by way of an incremental credit committee, which is a sub-committee of the TCC and which meets on an ongoing basis.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Education and Youth the measures being taken to provide suitable accommodation and teaching spaces for special education teachers in schools where supports are being delivered in corridors or other unsuitable locations.
reply:
While decisions on how school accommodation is used are a matter for individual school authorities, the department does not consider it appropriate to use corridors or other unsuitable areas of the school building to support children with special educational needs. I can confirm to the Deputy, that it is open to all schools to apply for capital funding under the Additional School Accommodation (ASA) scheme.
The purpose of my department’s Additional School Accommodation (or ASA) scheme is to ensure that essential mainstream classroom accommodation and accommodation for pupils with special education needs is available to cater for pupils enrolled each year, where the need cannot be met by the school’s existing accommodation or by available accommodation at other schools in the area.
Since 2020, my department has invested over €7 billion in our schools throughout the country under the National Development Plan, involving the completion of over 1,600 school building projects along with over 4,300 small-scale improvement works to meet priority maintenance needs and advance energy efficiency and climate goal. question: Deputy Willie O'Dea asked the Minister for Education and Youth if she is aware of the difficulties being experienced by many newly qualified post-primary teachers in attaining work in schools in order to complete the Droichead induction process; and whether she has any plans to make the Droichead induction process easier to access.
reply:
The recruitment and appointment of teachers to fill teaching posts is a matter for individual school authorities, subject to procedures agreed under Section 24 of the Education Act 1998 (as amended by the Education (Amendment) Act 2012). In that regard, there are more than 3,700 individual employers (boards of management of primary schools and post-primary schools, as well as ETBs).
While school authorities are the employer of teachers, the Department recognises the challenges faced by some teachers in securing employment and the impact that job insecurity can have on teachers’ wellbeing, financial stability, and long-term career planning.
In accordance with Department Circular 0044/2019, which is available on the Department’s website under www.gov.ie, schools are required to employ appropriately qualified teachers and ensure that unemployed teachers should be offered employment in preference to those who have retired.
Following on from the Department’s Action Plan on Teacher Supply, the Irish Primary Principals’ Network (IPPN) operates an online portal for the recruitment of teachers to long-term teaching positions. The portal facilitates the matching of demand and supply, and provides an efficient and user-friendly recruitment process for both schools and teachers.

This data includes, enrolment data, data on educational needs profiles (literacy and numeracy) and data on educational disadvantage. This data is sourced from within the education sector to ensure it is validated and assured. The only external data used is the Pobal HP Deprivation Index which is used by Irish government departments for identification of disadvantage.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade for an update on discussions regarding Moldova joining the European Union.
reply:
Ireland strongly supports EU enlargement, which is a key priority of our EU Presidency.
Moldova applied for EU membership in 2022 and opened accession negotiations in 2024. After completing the screening process, Moldova opened the first two negotiating clusters - Cluster 1 on Fundamentals and Clusters 6 on External Relations – in June and July respectively.
In July, during the first month of our Presidency, Ireland secured significant progress on the enlargement file, holding the highest number of accession conferences in a single day since 2002. In addition to opening cluster 6 with both Ukraine and Moldova, we facilitated the closure of two additional chapters with Montenegro as well as the closure of the first three negotiating chapters with Albania.
Last year, the European Commission's Enlargement Report highlighted that Moldova has made the most one-year progress of all the candidates over the reporting period. I am very conscious of the efforts that Moldova is making to meet the challenge of aligning their laws with the EU acquis, despite the ongoing hybrid threats and external interference they are facing.
As confirmed by the European Commission, Moldova, as well as Ukraine, is technically ready to open all negotiating clusters. As Presidency, Ireland will continue to engage with other Member States to secure the unanimity required for the opening of all remaining clusters with both Moldova and Ukraine.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the rationale behind recent changes to the SEN school transport escort payment guidelines whereby escorts are paid only for Department-approved journey time; if she acknowledges that many escorts are required to travel for significant periods before the first child is collected without remuneration; if she is concerned that this may worsen existing recruitment and retention difficulties in a service already experiencing shortages; and if she will review the policy to ensure escorts are fairly compensated for all time spent on duty in providing school transport for children.
reply:
The School Transport Scheme is a significant operation managed by Bus Éireann on behalf of the Department of Education and Youth.
There is a facility within the Special Educational Needs Transport Scheme for the appointment of a school transport escort where a child’s care and safety needs while on school transport are such as to require the support of a School Transport Escort.
The Board of Management/ETB are responsible for the employment of the school transport escort. The Department of Education and Youth provides grant funding directly to the school for the employment of the school transport escort and sets the rate of pay. question: Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Education and Youth the formal alternative infrastructure the State Examinations Commission is establishing to authenticate additional assessment components for home educated and medically vulnerable candidates without requiring them to self-source school permissions from schools who have not been given guidance on this scenario. .
reply:

Prior to the implementation of revised subject specifications and assessment arrangements under the Senior Cycle Redevelopment programme, 28 existing Leaving Certificate subjects already included assessment components beyond written examinations, including oral examinations, practical performance tests, and coursework. To protect examination integrity and ensure inter-candidate equity, the SEC advises that it requires all coursework to be authenticated. Coursework completion and authentication is an ongoing process of engagement and oversight over by class teachers, rather than a single ‘point in time’ engagement. question: Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her Department has plans to introduce a recourse mechanism for students who miss out on their CAO choice due to administrative errors by the State Examinations Commission such as not applying spelling and grammar waiver to a Leaving Certificate Examination paper.
reply:
The State Examinations Commission (SEC) has responsibility for the operation and delivery of State Examinations including facilitating access to these examinations via the Reasonable Accommodations at Certificate Examination (RACE) Scheme, which includes the waiver from the assessment of spelling, grammar and punctuation in language subjects.
In view of this, I have asked the SEC to respond directly to the Deputy with the requested information.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Education and Youth to urgently address issues raised in correspondence (details supplied) and allow for financial security/protections for young teachers, specifically maternity protection for teachers who have accumulated years of service but do not hold permanent contracts.
reply:
The Maternity Leave Scheme for teachers, as contained in the Department’s Circular Letter 0054/2019 (Chapter 2), is regulated by the Maternity Protection Act, 1994 as amended.
A teacher who is on a fixed term/fixed purpose contract of employment shall, during the term of the contract, have full leave entitlements in respect of statutory leaves and also may have entitlement to other leave types. The granting or taking of this leave should not affect a fixed term/fixed purpose appointment or the renewing of such an appointment. A teacher’s entitlement to leave shall cease on the expiry of a contract and that contract not having been renewed, unless that contract is followed directly by a ‘back to back’ contract in an approved teaching post funded by monies provided by the Oireachtas.
The recruitment and appointment of teachers to fill teaching posts is a matter for the individual school authority, subject to procedures agreed under Section 24 of the Education Act 1998 (as amended by the Education (Amendment) Act 2012). The agreed procedures are set out in the Department’s circulars.
In accordance with Department Circulars 0044/2019 (primary) and 0031/2011 (post primary), schools are required to employ appropriately qualified and registered teachers and ensure that unemployed teachers should be offered employment in preference to those who have retired.
The revised criteria governing the award of a Contract of Indefinite duration (CID) for teachers employed in the primary sector

question: Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the current measures and future plans being taken to strengthen the State’s capacity to provide emergency consular assistance and evacuation support to Irish citizens abroad during conflicts, natural disasters and other major crises; and whether lessons from recent international emergencies have identified any gaps in the current system.
reply:
My Department’s crisis governance framework provides clear guidance for the activation of an effective, timely and robust response to a range of crises, with a view to providing consular assistance to affected Irish citizens and their family members.
Indeed, the Deputy will be aware that during the recent crisis in the Middle East and Gulf, the most significant crisis since the COVID, officials from across my Department, offered direct consular assistance to almost 2900 people. This is the equivalent of an entire year’s worth of ‘normal’ consular assistance operations, and is a strong indicator that existing plans are more than fit for purpose.
Depending on the severity of the crisis, my Department can activate a variety of crisis response measure, including the creation of an emergency task team to ensure a whole of Department approach to any response; the strengthening of the core consular team and of relevant regional missions; and the activation of a surge team.
I can confirm that, at my instruction, my Department activated all these measures during the Middle East and Gulf crisis, which saw more than 100 officials working as part of the response, including to assist the return of 380 Irish citizens and their dependents to Ireland, with a focus on those must vulnerable.
I can assure the Deputy that planning to enhance our capacity to response is ongoing, including through an ongoing lessons learned process, which is currently considering detailed input from officials acro

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment his views on the development of a Basic Income Strategy for Ireland, particularly in the context of developments in Artificial Intelligence and other technologies.
reply:
The development of a Basic Income Strategy for Ireland is not under active consideration by my Department.
In 2022 the Low Pay Commission published their report on piloting Universal Basic Income (UBI). The report was accompanied by a report, authored by the ESRI under the terms of the Low Pay Commission / ESRI Research Partnership Agreement, titled ‘A universal basic income for Ireland: Lessons from the international literature’.
The ESRI report examined the universal basic income pilots that have taken place in other jurisdictions, what policy objectives a universal basic income pilot could address and its associated risks and financial implications.
In their report the Low Pay Commission noted that “the recommendations and guidelines in this report regarding how UBI might be piloted in Ireland should not be seen as an implicit endorsement of the concept of a UBI by the Low Pay Commission. The Low Pay Commission was not asked to evaluate the concept of a UBI. Nor was it asked to evaluate whether or not UBI should be piloted”.
The Commission’s report described five general principles that the Low Pay Commission recommended for the design of any UBI pilot for Ireland.
I note that in 2022 the Commission on Taxation and Welfare reported that “The Commission does not support the development of a Universal Basic Income in Ireland” and that “Further, it is noted that resourcing such a pilot project may detract from the State’s ability to fund means-tested welfare schemes, or other

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the way in which the Government is using or will use Artificial Intelligence to reduce inequality in society.
reply:
The Government recognises that while AI presents significant opportunities, it also poses certain challenges, including the potential to deepen existing inequalities if access to technology, skills and opportunities is uneven. A strong regulatory framework is also essential to ensure fundamental rights are protected.
For this reason, Ireland's National Digital & AI Strategy, Digital Ireland – Connecting our People, Securing our Future places a strong emphasis on digital inclusion, lifelong learning, workforce reskilling and the development of trustworthy AI systems that operate in accordance with European and national regulatory frameworks.
The Government's approach to AI is anchored in the EU AI Act, which takes a risk-based approach to ensure that AI systems used in the EU are safe, transparent and respect fundamental rights, including equality and non-discrimination.
The Act is expressly designed to reduce the risk that AI systems reinforce, amplify, or institutionalise harmful norms and stereotypes, by embedding principles of non-discrimination, fairness, transparency, human oversight, and bias mitigation into the development, provision and deployment of AI systems.
The Act prohibits certain practices that could deepen inequality, such as social scoring and AI systems that exploit people's vulnerabilities due to age, disability or social or economic circumstances. It also places strict requirements on high-risk AI systems, including those used in recruitment, workplace ma

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the projected 2026 overspend for each Department against its approved gross allocation; the total value of supplementary estimates expected to be sought before the end of 2026, in tabular form.
reply:
Gross voted spending at end August was €73.7 billion. This is €0.8 billion or 1.1% below the aggregate profile submitted by departments. Departments may be ahead or below profile for a variety of reasons. Deviations from profile may arise due to the timing of certain payments and these may correct themselves over the course of the year. Other overspends against profile may require mitigating actions to be taken to offset the overrun before year end.
It is the responsibility of each Accounting Officer to manage expenditure within their allocations approved by the Dáil. It is essential that departments actively pursue efficiencies and reforms to identify savings within their allocations, and to ensure that the significant resources allocated to them are used to efficiently and effectively deliver high-quality public services and supports.
In any given year, there can be a range of reasons why Departments might require supplementary funding above the amount included in the original estimate. Additional allocations may be needed due to in-year Government decisions to provide supports in response to developments or where services or schemes cost more than a department originally estimated.
My department actively monitors spending developments throughout the year and will continue to monitor and engage with Departments over the remainder of year to identify any spending risks and mitigations to these. The provision of any Supplementary Estimates is a matter for Government decision.

question: Deputy Noel McCarthy asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation to outline the progress made, and total cost to date, with respect to the upgrade of a Garda Station (details supplied).
reply:
I can confirm that the Office of Public Works (OPW) has undertaken refurbishment and Universal Access works to Cloyne Garda Station.
Works included Provision of a Universal Access ramp, 3 car parking spaces one of which is a universally accessible parking space; a new stepped access to the Garda station building; Universal Access Counter; internal upgrade.
The refurbishment works are substantially completed, with the OPW awaiting the completion of the Safety File from the contractor before the station can be handed over to An Garda Síochána.
The cost of the above works will be available when final account is complete.

question: Deputy Noel McCarthy asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation to outline plans for the renovation of a Garda station (details supplied); when the redevelopment is expected to begin; and the total amount currently earmarked for completion of the project.
reply:
I can confirm that the Office of Public Works (OPW) has scheduled refurbishment and Universal Access works to Youghal Garda Station.
Works will include the provision of a universal access ramp and entrance approach steps; the relocation and widening of the front entrance gate; external lighting; the replacement of the existing windows and doors; the application of external insulation to the exterior of the station with a paint finish; and other minor ancillary works.
The planned works are at pre-tender stage so the overall project estimated costings have not been finalised.
The commencement date for works are subject to statutory obligations, final sign-off on design, funding, and operational requirements of An Garda Síochána and the internal approval process of An Garda Síochána and OPW.

question: Deputy Eamon Scanlon asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation for an update on the development of the new Regional Veterinary Laboratory in Sligo and the appointment of a design team by OPW; the current status of the project; the anticipated timeline for planning, tendering and construction; and the expected completion date.
reply:
The new Sligo Regional Veterinary Laboratory (RVL) is part of a Regional Laboratory Redevelopment Programme which has been included in the National Development Plan and the Programme for Government, for the Department of Agriculture Food and the Marine.
The Sligo RVL project is currently at an early stage of development. The focus of the RVL programme to date has been directed to the development of the design, and obtaining planning approvals for the Kilkenny facility, which will serve as the exemplar design for the new Sligo scheme.
Given the early stage of development and balancing other organisational priorities, OPW are in the process of reviewing resources and may utilise external consultants to develop the design. It is too early to provide a timeline for planning approvals, tendering or construction, all of which will be influenced by the availability of capital funding and prioritisation by the Department of Agriculture Food and the Marine.
OPW will continue to engage with the relevant stakeholders as the project progresses and can provide further information on the anticipated programme and construction timelines when these matters have been sufficiently advanced.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation whether the projected 2026 Departmental overruns have been factored into the fiscal parameters for Budget 2027; the extent to which the overspend will be carried into 2027 allocations.
reply:
My Department actively monitors spending developments throughout the year and is in ongoing engagement with all other Departments to identify any spending risks and mitigations to these.
In any given year, there can be a range of reasons why Departments may require funding above the amount originally included in an Estimate. Additional allocations may be needed due to Government decisions to provide supports in response to developments during the year or where services or schemes cost more than a Department originally estimated. The additional funding may be required on temporary or reoccurring basis.
Incorporating all expenditure overruns facilitated through supplementary estimates into future years budgets would risk embedding inefficiencies into the base and undermine the need for meaningful reforms to be developed and implemented.
Government is providing €125.5 billion in voted expenditure for 2027, an increase of €7 billion compared to 2026. This is set out in the Summer Economic Statement 2026.
Expenditure allocations for each Department for 2027 are presently being finalised, with negotiations between my Department and other Departments still ongoing. Negotiations undertaken as part of the estimates process represent the culmination of ongoing analysis as well as significant discussions between Ministers and their officials.

question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation whether he has sought or received advice regarding a requirement (details supplied); whether the consumer and affordability implications of this requirement have been assessed by his Department or by the Regulator; and whether consideration has been given to permitting consumers to purchase a single line at the standard €2 per-line price.
reply:
I wish to inform the Deputy that responsibility for the operation of the National Lottery and implementation of changes to the Lotto game lies with the Operator (Premier Lotteries Ireland DAC).
The requirement in the National Lottery that players purchase a minimum of two Lotto lines has been part of the Lotto game rules for over 30 years. Changes to the Lotto game have been introduced periodically over the years following a review of the game by the Operator (An Post National Lottery Company and subsequently Premier Lotteries Ireland DAC) and approval through the appropriate regulatory process in place at the time (i.e. now the Regulator for the National Lottery) as being compliant with the legal framework. Changes have included, for example: guaranteed minimum jackpots, an additional draw day, additional prize tiers, additional balls, and ticket price increases. Each time, the aim is to support the long-term sustainability of Lotto while continuing to provide players with an engaging game experience.
The most recent changes to Lotto, in September, are the first significant changes in ten years. They follow a detailed review of the game by the Operator, included research into Lotto players’ preferences. The changes include, for the first time, the removal of two number balls from the game to improve the odds of winning a prize at each tier, including the jackpot. Ticket prices per line are unchanged.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the level of regulation in place on Buy Now Pay Later and flexible payment plan options offered on apps and online such as (details supplied).
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 259, 260 and 261 together.

The Central Bank's Consumer Protection Code applies in full to BNPL. This ensures that customers of these credit providers are afforded the same protections as customers of other credit providers.
New rules signed into Irish law in July of this year under the European Union’s Directive 2023/2673 further strengthen the protections for consumers purchasing financial products or services online or by phone.

question: Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade to provide an update on Ireland’s engagement with international partners in responding to the ongoing conflict and humanitarian crisis in Sudan.
reply:
The conflict in Sudan has created the world’s worst humanitarian, displacement and protection crisis. Yet it has not garnered the level of international attention, and sustained political engagement, that its scale and severity demand. The Government continues to use our influence in the EU and the UN to raise awareness and to call for and end to the conflict and support for efforts for a Sudanese-led transition to civilian rule.
We are members of the Coalition for Atrocity Prevention and Justice in Sudan alongside Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, Sierra Leone, and the UK. We have also highlighted the situation in Sudan regularly at the current session of the Human Rights Council in Geneva.
At the UN General Assembly in New York last week, the Taoiseach, the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade and I spoke clearly on the situation in Sudan. Delivering Ireland's national statement at the General Assembly, the Taoiseach called on the international community to act more decisively to bring an end to the conflict.
I attended two important Sudan events during the week in New York. At the Sudan Ministerial Meeting, convened by the EU, African Union, France, Germany, UK and US, I underlined Ireland’s support for diplomatic efforts to advance a civilian political dialogue process. question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will consider a tax credit or relief for childcare and school age childcare costs for working lone parents; the estimated full year cost of such a measure at various rates.
reply:
The Government acknowledges the cost pressures on families and parents with young children. In recognition of these pressures, several support measures are already in place to ease the burden on working parents.
The personal income tax packages implemented by the previous Government, have made significant progress on increasing the entry point to income tax for all income earners and increasing the point at which the higher rate of income tax takes effect.
As the Deputy will be aware, to ease the burden facing average and middle-income earners, over successive Budgets the previous Government substantially increased the entry point to the higher rate of income tax for all earners by €8,700 or c. 25 per cent. The main tax credits have also been increased by €350, or c. 21 per cent. In line with the Government policy of ensuring full-time workers on the minimum wage remain outside the charge to the top rates of USC the ceiling of the 2 per cent USC rate band was increased by €6,898, or 34 per cent, from 2020 to 2025. Budgets 2024 and 2025 also cumulatively reduced the 4.5 per cent rate of USC to 3 per cent.
Broadly, the income tax measures implemented over the period of the last Government are expected to be in line with wage growth.
Section 462B of the Taxes Consolidation Act 1997 provides for the Single Person Child Carer Tax Credit (“SPCCC”). The SPCCC is available to a single person who proves that they have a qualifying child resident with them for the whole or greater part

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the total amount of tax revenue received by the State from the private rental sector in each of the years 2020 to 2025 and to date in 2026, including income tax, corporation tax, capital gains tax and any other relevant taxation receipts; the extent to which his Department separately records taxation receipts attributable to the private rental sector.
reply:
I am advised by Revenue that, due to the manner in which various taxes are administered, there is no data available from which to identify tax receipts attributable solely to the private rental sector.
I am informed by Revenue that an income tax liability is calculated on taxpayers’ total income from all sources, rather than being separately calculated for each source of income (such as rental income) and having regard to any relevant reliefs or credits. For this reason, it is not possible to identify income tax paid arising from rental income alone.
However, the Deputy may be interested to note that publications which outline the total amount of rental income and total net profit declared by chargeable persons by year for 2016-2023, broken down by residential and commercial properties, are available at the following link: www.revenue.ie/en/corporate/information-about-revenue/statistics/income-distributions/rental-income.aspx. The data for 2024 will be published shortly at the same link. Chargeable persons are required to file their 2025 Form 11 tax returns no later than 31 October 2026, with an extension for ROS filers until 18 November 2026. Data for 2025 will be available when these returns have been processed and fully analysed.
I am further informed by Revenue that non-trading income is taxable at the 25% corporation tax rate. Non trading income includes rental income as well as other income streams such as investment income. A corporation tax liability is not calculated

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance to list specific examples from January 2020 to date of where he or his predecessors have followed advice (details supplied).
reply:
The Irish Fiscal Advisory Council plays a key role in our budgetary process and their analysis is always considered by Government.
It is, of course, impossible to exactly quantify the impact the Fiscal Council has made to economic and fiscal discourse in Ireland, which in turn informs Government policy. However, a non-exhaustive list of the number of ways the Council have meaningfully contributed to the formulation of fiscal policy in recent years is presented below.
First of all, each year, the Council assess and endorse my Department’s spring and autumn macroeconomic forecasts, which underpin policy decisions. This thorough and demanding exercise has contributed to improvements in the Department’s forecasting methodologies including the introduction of the Department’s methodology for producing estimates of the supply-side of the economy.
On top of this, the Council has been a strong advocate on the need for multi-annual budgeting for a number of years. In December 2025, the Government published its Medium-Term Fiscal and Structural Plan. The publication of the Plan represents a fundamental shift in the way budgetary policy is formulated in Ireland, pivoting towards medium-term budgeting. Crucially, the Plan means we fixed spending ceilings for the rest of the decade.

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance his views that the current eligibility criteria for a primary medical certificate (PMC) under the disabled drivers and disabled passengers scheme, results in an inequity whereby persons who are blind or severely visually impaired do not qualify for the scheme despite facing significant mobility and transport challenges; if he will engage with the Minister of State with responsibility for Disability to review and amend the regulations governing the scheme to include persons with severe visual impairments.
reply:
My Department and I share concerns that the Disabled Drivers and Disabled Passengers Scheme or DDS is no longer fit-for-purpose. Following extensive review of the DDS, the Government has now agreed to commence from early 2027 the Department of Transport’s Vehicle Adaptation Scheme (VAS). The VAS will provide direct financial assistance to all individuals with qualifying vehicle adaptation needs to meet the costs of those adaptations. The VAS will improve individuals’ functional mobility that in turn can contribute to better social and economic opportunities.
It is important to recognise that broader Government commitments to transport solutions for those with a disability are essential and are distinct from meeting vehicle adaption needs.
The Disabled Drivers and Disabled Passengers Scheme (DDS) remains with the Department of Finance and will be kept under review. Learning from the commencement and initial operation of the VAS will further inform reform options for the DDS.
As the Deputy will be aware, when this government took office, we committed to a step change in the delivery of supports and services for people with disability and their families.
Budget 2026 is the first step in delivering on this ambition, providing some €3.83 billion to specialist disability services next year, an unprecedented increase of €618 million, or almost 20%.
This funding will be vital in delivering the National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People. The commitment to develop a new scheme

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Transport the supports available for the installation of electric vehicle charging points at further and higher education institutions.
reply:

€170m has been allocated in 2026 to support the continued transition to EVs which includes funding for EV grants and EV charging infrastructure. This underpins the Government's commitment to making electric vehicles accessible to all.

• a €3,500 purchase grant for battery electric vehicles (BEVs) up to €50,000 in value
• a home charging grant scheme, with over 32,000 applications approved or paid in 2026

• benefit-in-kind tax relief for BEVs
• VRT relief of up to €5,000 for BEVs
• a low rate of annual motor tax
• the ICE2EV pilot scrappage scheme
From a business perspective there are also supports available including:
• a grant for taxi drivers to make the switch to an EV
• a fleet assessment grant to help businesses explore the transition to EVs
• a grant for HDVs and associated infrastructure to bridge the gap between a zero emission vehicle and a fossil fuel vehicle.
There are currently no dedicated Government grant schemes specifically targeted at the installation of electric vehicle c

question: Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Transport for an update on the proposed development of a Road Safety Commissioner as part of reforms to strengthen road safety governance and oversight; and to outline the progress made in considering the role, functions and statutory basis of such a Commissioner. .
reply:
The current framework for road safety governance is set out in the Government’s Road Safety Strategy 2021–2030 and its Phase 2 Action Plan 2025–2027. The Strategy follows the internationally recognised Safe System approach, under which responsibility is shared across the relevant road safety bodies working in partnership.
My Department coordinates implementation of the Strategy. Oversight is provided by the Road Safety Leadership Group, which I chair and which includes the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration and senior representatives of the principal road safety partners. The Group reviews delivery and progress on a quarterly basis.
Within that framework, no decision has been taken to establish a Road Safety Commissioner and detailed proposals on the role, functions or statutory basis of such an office have not been developed.
My focus as Minister, the focus of my Department and of all the road partners with whom we work with, is on the delivery of the Phase 2 Action Plan through the existing governance and oversight arrangements. I will, however, continue to consider proposals that have a clear potential to improve road safety outcomes.

question: Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Transport for an update on the ongoing expansion of average-speed and static safety cameras on the national road network; the number of additional cameras planned, their expected deployment timeframe; and the consideration being given to further expansion on high-risk routes.
reply:
Camera based enforcement, like all enforcement of road traffic offences, is primarily the responsibility of An Garda Síochána. To assist An Garda Síochána in this work, the National Safety Camera Strategy was developed and published on the 29th of April of this year. The Strategy aligns with Programme for Government commitments to expand the use of safety cameras across the road network and also delivers on part one of Action 6 of the Government’s Road Safety Strategy Phase 2 Action Plan 2025 - 2027.
The Strategy provides the framework for the increased deployment of cameras across the network, in both urban and rural locations, to assist with the enforcement of a wide range of road traffic offences. It focuses on speeding, red light running, and bus lane infringements, with flexibility for the enforcement of other types of offence in future.
A Camera Enforcement Oversight Group has been established to deliver the Strategy, chaired by the CEO of the National Transport Authority (NTA) and comprising senior leaders from An Garda Síochána, NTA, Transport Infrastructure Ireland, the Road Safety Authority, the Courts Service and the Local Authority sector. The Oversight Group has met twice, on the 16th of June and the 5th of August and I expect a progress update to be presented at the next Road Safety Leadership Group meeting.

question: Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Transport the current status of the National Vehicle and Driver File, Road Traffic and Roads Bill 2026; the remaining steps required before its enactment; and the timeframe within which he expects the Bill to be enacted. .
reply: The National Vehicle and Driver File, Road Traffic and Roads Bill 2026 passed Second Stage in the Dáil on 17 September 2026. question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Transport his plans to engage with TII for the purpose of extending Luas operating hours past midnight, and introducing a permanent late-night Luas service.

question: Deputy Michael Fitzmaurice asked the Minister for Transport when the independent appeals process will be in place for applicants who have been refused payment under the road transport support scheme.
reply:
My Department will announce the date for the opening of the Road Transporters Support Scheme (RTSS) appeals process in the coming days. Applicants are encouraged to monitor the RTSS webpage for updates on the appeals process.
Only applicants that have a valid RTSS Application ID will be permitted to submit an appeal. Applicants may request an appeal if an application has been refused or if support was not provided for one or more vehicles included on an application. Submitting an appeal does not guarantee that it will be successful, and each appeal will be assessed on its own merits and in accordance with the appeals eligibility criteria.
Applicants are encouraged to review the appeals process terms and conditions and eligibility criteria in full once they are publicly available and gather any relevant supporting documentation before the appeals portal opens. All appeals must be supported by evidence. My Department will not consider an appeal submitted without supporting evidence.

question: Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Transport if he plans to reduce toll costs or implement a refund scheme for students commuting to universities via driving on motorways.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for overall policy and funding in relation to the national roads programme. Under the Roads Acts 1993-2015, the operation and management of individual national roads is a matter for Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII), in conjunction with the local authorities concerned.
Therefore, matters relating to the day to day operations regarding national roads, including toll roads are within the remit of TII. More specifically, the statutory power to levy tolls, to make toll bye-laws and to enter into agreements with private investors are vested in TII under Part V of the Roads Act 1993 (as amended). The contracts for the privately-operated toll schemes are commercial agreements between TII and the Public Private Partnership (PPP) concessionaires concerned.
At present I have no plans to review tolling policy towards any particular group of road users. It must be borne in mind also that toll revenue is a key income stream for funding for protection and renewal of our road network, and accordingly any reduction in toll revenue would require additional funding to be raised elsewhere to maintain the current level of investment.

reply:
Under the Regional and Local Roads Grant Programme, there is no specific winter maintenance allocation made to local authorities.
The allocation made to the programme's Discretionary Grant, allows eligible local authorities to exercise discretion in its use for eligible winter maintenance work. In accordance with Section 13 of the Roads Act 1993, as amended, the improvement and maintenance of regional and local roads is the statutory responsibility of each local authority. Work on such roads is funded from Councils' own resources, supplemented by State road grants. The initial selection and prioritisation of work to be funded is a matter for local authorities.
As Minister for Transport I have responsibility for overall policy and exchequer funding in relation to the National Roads Programme. Under the Roads Acts 1993-2015 and in line with the National Development Plan (NDP), the operation and management of individual national roads is a matter for Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII), in conjunction with the local authorities concerned. This is also subject to the Infrastructure Guidelines and the necessary statutory approvals.

question: Deputy John Clendennen asked the Minister for Transport if his Department is aware of difficulties reportedly experienced by Irish motor insurance policyholders seeking to temporarily add visiting non-EU licence holders as named drivers, including cases where insurer systems are unable to process foreign driving-licence numbers or international driving permits; and whether all insurers are expected to have arrangements to record and validate the licence number or other unique identifier of a foreign licence holder for the purposes of the Irish Motor Insurance Database.
reply:
Under section 78A of the Road Traffic Act 1961, as amended, the Motor Insurers’ Bureau of Ireland (MIBI) is responsible for maintaining the Irish Motor Insurance Database (IMID). The data contained in the IMID is provided by motor insurers, brokers, fleet owners and motor traders, and includes policyholder details, vehicle registration numbers and the names of drivers authorised to drive vehicles covered by a policy.
Section 78A(2)(f)(ii)(III) of the Act provides that, for drivers who hold a foreign driving licence, the relevant driver identifier may be recorded using the driver number, licence number or another unique identifier, as appropriate. A proportion of the driver numbers recorded on the IMID relates to individuals who hold non-Irish driving licences. All such driver numbers must be validated manually by the relevant insurance provider.
The Department’s attention was first drawn to reports of difficulties experienced by holders of non-EU driving licences being added as named drivers on motor insurance policies last week. In light of these reports, the Department contacted MIBI to establish whether any operational issues had arisen in relation to the implementation of the legislative requirements governing the IMID. The Department was informed that no issues relating to non-Irish driving licences had been reported to MIBI.

question: Deputy James O'Connor asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the number of staff that are currently accredited to the embassy of the Russian Federation.
reply:
Despite Ireland's fundamental disagreement with the actions taken by the Russian Federation since its unjustified and illegal full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the Government's view is that diplomatic channels between Ireland and the Russian Federation should remain open.
This is in the interests of our citizens, in Russia and in the four Central Asian countries to which Ireland is accredited via our Embassy in Moscow. This also allows us to continue to formally convey the Government's strong objection to the illegal and unwarranted war of aggression by Russia against Ukraine.
The Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, 1961 identifies three categories of staff of a diplomatic mission: diplomatic staff, administrative and technical staff and service staff.
There are currently 17 staff members at the Embassy of the Russian Federation in Ireland who have been notified to my Department under Article 10 of the Convention - six Diplomats and 11 Administrative and Technical staff. The current number of staff accredited to the Embassy is taken at a point in time, and minor increases or decreases in numbers may relate to vacancies that arise over time.
Prior to Russia’s illegal invasion of Ukraine there were a total of 30 staff at the Embassy, 14 diplomats and 16 Administrative and Technical staff.

question: Deputy Michael Collins asked the Minister for Defence if she will provide a breakdown of the average number of days paid to Defence Force personnel in the Army Reserve for 2026, excluding courses and annual training of five days or more (details supplied).
reply:
My key priority is the modernisation of our Defence Forces, and revitalising our Reserve Defence Force is a vital part of that transformation process. This is reflected in the substantial expansion of the RDF budget which continues to increase in pace with the enhanced role of the RDF. To illustrate this, the budget allocation in 2025 was €3.542m, with 28,922 Reserve Training and Support Days (RTSD's) undertaken, and I have further increased it to €4.535m for 2026.
In 2026, 18,913 RTSDs were undertaken between 1 January and 31 May and this includes both training and support activities.
On 1 June, I welcomed the introduction of Supplemental Military Service (SMS) for the Reserve Defence Force (RDF) which regularises RDF activities to support the Permanent Defence Force. The introduction of SMS for members of the RDF updates a previous administrative system to ensure consistency with the provisions of the Defence (Amendment) Act 2021. Therefore, from 1 June, Reserve Training Days and SMS replaced RTSDs. Since 1 June, RDF members were paid a total of 14,687 RTDs and 3,893 SMS days.
The further breakdown of these figures, as requested by the Deputy, is not recorded in the manner sought by the Deputy. Unfortunately it is therefore not possible to provide a response in that regard.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment with regard to energised grid-scale lithium-ion battery energy storage system (Li-BESS) installations in the State, if Ireland has designated the competent authority and notifying authority required under Regulation (EU) 2023/1542; if so, to identify those authorities; the dates on which they were designated; if not, when such designations will be made.
reply:
Article 54 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 on batteries and waste batteries requires Member States to designate one or more competent authorities responsible for obligations relating to the management of waste batteries. Ireland has designated the competent authorities for these purposes through national implementing regulations signed on 20 April 2026. There is, however, no requirement under the EU Regulation to designate a competent authority specifically for the operation or oversight of battery energy storage energy systems.
Separately, Article 22 of the EU Regulation requires Member States to designate a notifying authority. The role of the notifying authority is to assess, notify and monitor conformity assessment bodies. It does not itself assess or approve individual batteries or battery energy storage system installations.
While Ireland’s Notifying Authority has not yet been designated, work is ongoing within the Department to put in place the necessary structures to ensure its functions can be discharged effectively.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment with regard to energised grid-scale Li-BESS installation in the State, the mandatory operational safety standards that apply; and the act or statutory instruments which are imposed and enforceable.
reply:
All batteries used in grid-connected Lithium-ion battery electricity storage systems (li-BESS) on the Irish grid are manufactured, sold and operated in line with EU regulation and standards. This includes safety certification and labelling for the marketing and the putting into service of batteries used in grid-connected electrical storage systems.
Batteries, including those integrated within energy storage systems, may only be placed on the EU market or put into service if they meet all the applicable requirements as determined by a Conformity Assessment Body. The Conformity Assessment Bodies are subject to assessment and monitoring by a Notifying Authority.
The EU Batteries Regulation 1542/2023 requires that a conformity assessment procedure be carried out in respect of batteries placed on the market to demonstrate, inter alia, compliance with safety requirements.
The procedure is intended to ensure compliance with provisions covering the safety of grid-connected stationary battery electricity storage systems such as those under Article 12 of the Regulation, where such systems must be subject to appropriate testing and potential safety hazards must be assessed and tested with appropriate mitigation measures and instructions in place.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if an allowance will be considered for newer homes that have already completed solar upgrades in terms of retrospectively providing grant support in the interest of fairness and in the context of forthcoming changes to eligibility for the SEAI grant (details supplied).
reply:
My Department funds a number of grant schemes, administered by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI), to support homeowners to improve the energy efficiency of their existing properties.
These schemes have terms and conditions in place to ensure the transparent administration of public funds. These terms and conditions must be adhered to consistently by the SEAI to ensure fairness as well as value for money for the Exchequer.
Grant assistance for residential retrofitting measures provided by Government through these schemes is intended to incentivise future behaviour. Homeowners who have not applied and been approved for grant support through the SEAI prior to commencing works on their properties are not entitled to retrospective awarding of SEAI grants. While my Department, in partnership with the SEAI, continues to ensure that grant schemes terms and conditions, eligibility criteria, and rates are kept under review, taking account of demand, research, innovation, evolving technology and other relevant factors, there are no plans to change the eligibility criteria in terms of retrospectively providing grant support as set out by the Deputy.

question: Deputy Edward Timmins asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the progress that will be made on implementing the Draghi report during Ireland's Presidency.
reply:
The Government strongly supports the EU’s competitiveness agenda. The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade holds horizontal responsibility for EU Policy across government, including coordination of our response to the Draghi and Letta Reports, and the new One Europe, One Market Roadmap. This is a whole of government effort, with the negotiations in Brussels and the domestic implementation resting with the relevant lead Departments.
Ireland’s experience of Europe’s Single Market as an engine for transformational economic growth has shaped our approach to EU policy-making. This is why competitiveness is one of our three core pillars during our Council Presidency term.
Central to this is our commitment to take forward work on the One Europe, One Market Roadmap, an inter-institutional agreement focused on the competitiveness agenda and which was signed by leaders in April of this year.
The Roadmap seeks to translate the ambition to close Europe’s competitiveness gap, as expressed in the Draghi and Letta Reports and the Competitiveness Compass, into 42 key identified measures and targets across five key pillars. The new framework takes forward the recommendations of the Draghi and Letta reports and seeks to implement many of measures and proposals identified in these reports.
The Roadmap also sets out ambitious timelines and deadlines for the agreement of proposals under our Presidency, which will be vital to boosting European competitiveness and building our economic resilienc

reply:

question: Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he will clarify whether the European Commission has issued any communication or reasoned opinion to Ireland regarding incomplete transposition of Directive (EU) 2023/1791, with particular reference to Article 12 on data centres; the date of such correspondence and Ireland's response; if he will outline the financial penalties if the matter is referred to the Court of Justice of the European Union.
reply:
The European Commission issued a Letter of Formal Notice to Ireland on 20 November 2025 in relation to the incomplete transposition of Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency. Ireland submitted a response to the Commission on 19 January 2026 outlining the position in relation to the matters raised. Ireland has already notified the Commission of the transposition of 6 articles from this Directive, and work is continuing to finalise the transposition of the remainder.
Ireland has continued to engage with the Commission on the transposition of the Directive including through two subsequent engagements during which the Commission was updated on progress made.
No Reasoned Opinion has been issued to Ireland in respect of this matter. With regard to Article 12 of the Directive, concerning data centres, work is ongoing to finalise the necessary transposing legislation, which is expected to be signed into law in Q4 2026.
Ireland remains committed to completing the transposition of the Directive and continues to engage constructively with the European Commission in this regard.

question: Deputy Noel McCarthy asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the measures being taken by his Department to encourage households with solar panels to sell excess electricity back to the grid and if any phasing out or reduction in the current energy credit system is being considered.
reply:
The Domestic Solar PV Grant Scheme under the Micro-generation Support Scheme (MSS) provides grants through the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) towards the cost of installing solar PV panels.
The solar PV scheme has, as at end August 2026, supported over 21,000 homes install solar PV panels this year, and over 35,000 applications have been received (72% increase in applications year on year). This indicates that the scheme is working very well and that householders are recognising the benefits of investing in solar PV.
Exporting excess electricity to the grid typically yields a lower financial return than using it yourself. Hence, using the electricity you generate is the most efficient way to get the best return on your investment.
I am pleased to say that just this week I announced a Government approved package of enhanced renewable energy and retrofit grants which included a grant for battery storage systems and extended eligibility of solar PV and solar thermal grants to houses built and occupied pre-2025 which will further expand accessibility to the grant and promote solar PV installations.

question: Deputy Donnchadh Ó Laoghaire asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade her views on the war in Sudan and the Government's position regarding same.
reply:
The Government remains deeply concerned by the conflict in Sudan, which has created the world’s worst humanitarian, displacement and protection crisis. At the UN General Assembly in New York last week, the Taoiseach, the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade, and I, engaged extensively on Sudan. Delivering Ireland's national statement at the General Assembly, the Taoiseach called on the international community to act more decisively to bring an end to the conflict.
I also participated in a Sudan Ministerial Meeting, convened by the EU, African Union, France, Germany, UK and US, to advance diplomatic efforts towards a civilian political dialogue process. I also joined an event, hosted by the Coalition for Atrocity Prevention and Justice in Sudan, which focused on the protection of civilians and humanitarian personnel. I am deeply concerned by the increasing use of deadly drone strikes in Sudan, which is causing further civilian suffering, disrupting humanitarian assistance, and compounding an already devastating humanitarian crisis. It is imperative to maintain sustained and coordinated political pressure on all parties to the conflict, including external actors, to comply with their obligations under international law.

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the steps her Department is taking to reach the 0.7% goal for Overseas Development Aid; and the engagements she has with other EU member states on increasing their Aid budgets.
reply:
The Government remains committed to the United Nations target to provide 0.7% of Gross National Income (GNI) in Official Development Assistance (ODA). This commitment was reaffirmed in A Better World, Ireland's international development policy and in the Programme for Government which commits to increases in ODA, towards the 0.7% target, as part of the annual budgeting process.
Ireland’s total ODA amounted to €1.88 billion in 2025, representing 0.44% of GNI. In recent years, the Government has consistently increased the allocation for the Irish Aid programme managed by the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, which works to address the needs of some of the world’s poorest or most climate-exposed countries and communities and those living in areas affected by conflict. Budget 2026 provided for an allocation of just over €840 million, the highest in the 52-year history of the Irish Aid programme.
Ahead of Budget 2027, I am working with colleagues to ensure an ODA allocation which can continue to deliver on our commitment to development cooperation and to reaching the furthest behind first.
The Government has prioritised development cooperation and humanitarian assistance during our EU Presidency, in engagements within the EU and at the United Nations. question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the steps her Department is taking to support the work of the International Criminal Court and to oppose the sanctions currently being imposed on Judges and Prosecutors in the ICC by the United States.
reply:
Ireland is a strong supporter of the International Criminal Court (ICC), which we view as the cornerstone of the international system of criminal justice. I deeply regret the imposition of US sanctions against thirteen officials of the ICC. Such measures threaten to corrode the international legal order on which all states – but particularly small states like Ireland – depend.
I am aware of ongoing reports that the United States is considering sanctioning the ICC as an institution, which would very significantly impede the operational capacity of the Court. The ICC must be allowed to continue its important work, independently and impartially.
Ireland has been consistent in calling for all measures against the ICC to be withdrawn. The Taoiseach reiterated this principled position during his address to the UN General Assembly during UN High Level Week on 24 September. I look forward to underlining Ireland’s continued support for the ICC when I welcome ICC President, Judge Tomoko Akane, to Dublin on 5 October.
The Government believes that a coordinated EU response is the most effective way to protect the ICC and its officials. In our role as President of the EU Council, Ireland is committed to playing its part in maintaining full solidarity with the Court at this crucial moment.

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if a child born to an Irish parent abroad is entitled to Irish citizenship where the parent was also born abroad; the circumstances in which that birth must be registered in the Foreign Births Register in order to obtain a passport; if the requirement to register the birth in the Foreign Births Register to obtain a passport is waived in cases where the child has grandparents who are Irish citizens born in Ireland or in cases where there is difficulty obtaining a passport from another country to allow the child to travel home to Ireland.
reply:
Entitlement to Irish citizenship is determined by the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended, under which Irish citizenship may be obtained by birth, by descent, or by naturalisation.
If a person was born outside of Ireland, they may become an Irish citizen if:
• One of their grandparents was born in Ireland, or;
• One of their parents was an Irish citizen at the time of the person’s birth, even though that parent was not born in Ireland.
In these cases, a person can apply to become an Irish citizen through Foreign Birth Registration. Such applicants must be entered on the Foreign Birth Register before they can apply for a passport.
My Department is responsible for processing Foreign Birth Registration (FBR) applications. FBR applications are currently being processed within a turnaround time of 12 months from receipt of supporting documents. Applications that require further supporting documents will take longer to process.
Foreign Birth Registration, by its nature, is a detailed and complex process, often involving official documentation relating to three generations and issued by several jurisdictions. Such documents take considerable time to validate.
The FBR service operates a transparent general policy of processing applications in order of receipt except in cases of exceptional urgency, such as expectant parents, or stateless persons.
